speechtext:
On Monday last I advised the house that I would be able in a few days to make an announcement with respect to a payment by the Canadian wheat board on oats.
Effective at all country elevators in the prairie provinces on March 21, the initial
payment on all grades of oats will be increased by seven cents per bushel. The present initial payment for No. 2 C.W. oats is 65 cents per bushel and for No. 1 feed oats 60 cents per bushel. On and after March 21 the initial prices for these grades will be 72 cents and 67 cents per bushel, both prices basis in store Fort William/Port Arthur.
Producers who delivered oats to the Canadian wheat board between August 1, 1954, and the close of business on March 19, 1955, will receive an adjustment payment of 7 cents per bushel. This payment will follow immediately the completion of the adjustment payment on barley announced on Monday. This adjustment payment is of course subject to the 1 per cent P.F.A.A. levy.
During the period from August 1, 1954, to March 19, 1955, it is estimated that producers will have delivered about 47 million bushels of oats to the wheat board and therefore the adjustment payment on oats will involve the distribution to producers of about $3,290,000. In addition, the higher initial payment will be available to producers at country elevators from March 21 to the end of the crop year.
In the barley adjustment payment announced on Monday last and in the oats payment announced today, producers will receive over $11 million. These payments will be completed well before seeding and, as previously announced, will be followed by a final payment on the 1953-54 wheat pool.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) asked

Inquiries of the Ministry if in connection with the interprovincial conference there have been received in the recent past from any of the provinces representations to the effect that the economic committee set up at the 1945-1946 conference should meet in advance of the dominion-provincial conference, and if so what attitude the dominion government took to that suggestion. I said that I had no recollection of there being any such representations but that I should like to see the correspondence before making a formal assertion to that effect. I have looked at it and I find no reference to it. The hon. member was referring no doubt to the economic committee that was set up and operated, while the conference adjourned, for the purpose of preparing for the resumption of the discussions. I would expect that it would be normal that at our preliminary meeting such a committee would be set up to make preparations for the resumption of the discussions at the main federal-provincial conference. speechtext: I wonder whether I might ask the Prime Minister a further question. I believe, Mr. Chairman, there is only one question that really needs to be examined here. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT BRINGING ACT INTO FORCE ON APRIL 1, 1955
speechtext:
With regard to the first point that was raised by my hon. friend, I might say that some days ago the free copies of the separate volume of the new Criminal Code and related statutes which we are distributing to the judges and magistrates were sent out by the queen's printer. Since last year's annual statutes were published, the text of the Criminal Code in those statutes has been available in both English and French. The French language version of the aforesaid separate volume will go out on or before the date on which the act comes into force. I feel, therefore, there is no question as to the availability of copies.
With regard to the second point which my hon. friend raised, I do not believe he raised it too seriously so we will not change the date.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT BRINGING ACT INTO FORCE ON APRIL 1, 1955
speechtext:
I understand that the purpose of the one and only section in this bill is to provide for the coming into force of the Criminal Code by statute as well as by
[Mr. Gillis.)
proclamation, as was the government's original intention. That being the case, there does not seem to be much that can be said or done about it. I am ready .to confess that I scratched my head quite a bit and that I studied the books of procedure to see if there was any way in which one could amend this clause to delay the coming into force of some parts of the code, because there are some sections that we do not like. I have to add this further confession, that there does not seem to be any such way.
I gather that even if this bill were defeated, the Criminal Code would come into force by virtue of the proclamation already made, as provided in section 752 of the act that was passed during the last session of parliament. This bill simply confirms that proclamation. Since it is known we still dislike some of the provisions of the code which this bill brings into effect on April 1, namely sections 365, 372 and a few others, perhaps all we can do is register our protest in a formal way. In view of how we feel about it, I ask the minister not to ask for third reading of this bill today.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AGREEMENT RESPECTING TRACKS IN TORONTO HARBOUR AREA
speechtext:
This resolution seeks to introduce a bill to approve an agreement between the Toronto harbour commissioners, the Toronto Terminals Railway Company, Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway Company. As some hon. members know, the Toronto harbour commissioners constructed railway tracks on lands owned by the commissioners in the city of Toronto for the purpose of serving industries located in the harbour area. Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway Company have been operating their trains over these tracks for the purpose of

handling traffic to and from these industries. As the harbour commissioners did not have sufficient funds to maintain the tracks, they approached the railways with the object of having them take over the rehabilitation and maintenance thereof.
An agreement was entered into on October 5, 1954, whereby the Toronto Terminals Railway Company agreed to perform the work of rehabilitation of the existing tracks and maintain the same. The money required for this work was to be collected from Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway Company in the sum of $1.50 for each loaded car moved in or out of the harbour area.
The Toronto Terminals Railway is owned by Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway Company jointly. This company however has no power to enter into an agreement to maintain the railway of another company. And therefore it is necessary to have this legislation to authorize it to carry out the obligations under the agreement dated October 5, 1954. If I am permitted to say so at this time, I wish to inform hon. members that it is our intention to move that the proposed bill be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, when it has received second reading.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to delay the house to any extent with reference to this matter, except to say that this bill in its present form is in keeping with a habit that is being formed by the government, and evidenced by some of the legislation introduced in the house, whereby a bill containing certain features that are desirable has incorporated within it other amendments that are not desirable, in the view of some hon. members.
I refrain from going into the detail that was gone into at the resolution stage. All I wish to say on this occasion is that, having regard to those portions of the bill that have to do with the alteration or change in the grading of durum wheat, no objection can be taken. With regard to the question of overages, so far as public terminal elevators are concerned, there can be no objection. Indeed that section does not go as far as many of us feel it should go in order that provision might be made for the very large amount of overages piled up from year to year in the operations of the elevators taking in the wheat in the various marketing towns and villages of the western provinces.
However, we do take very strong objection with regard to the increase in the salaries of the commissioners, when regard is had to the recent appointment of Mr. Loptson to the board. This matter was fully discussed at the resolution stage. I am not going to rehearse what was said on a previous occasion; but I must say that, after having listened to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) respecting the appoint-of Mr. Loptson, it was indeed a remarkable example of psychic phenomena that Mr. Loptson's name should have been chosen by the Minister of Trade and Commerce before the minister had any idea whatsoever that this gentleman, if not actively engaged in

Canada Grain Act
politics in Saskatchewan, nevertheless was sufficiently actively engaged that he was a member of the Liberal party and the son of the former acting leader in the legislature, a fact which must have come as a great surprise, if not one to cause considerable astonishment, to the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Those coincidences, sir, do not happen very often. But, after all, that is why the word "coincidence" is in the dictionary-because sometimes coincidences do happen. And in this instance, when Mr. Loptson's name was finally decided upon by the Minister of Trade and Commerce it was found, on closer examination, that he possessed further qualifications than were known to exist at the time the decision was made.
We believe this appointment does not represent a desirable trend. And, believing that, although in favour of portions of the bill before the house, we find ourselves in a position where, in order to register our opposition to this kind of thing, we intend to oppose the bill in its present stage.
The board of grain commissioners performs a tremendously important role in the preservation of the rules of the game in the marketing of grains. Above everything else we believe, and it has been my contention for several years, going back to 1942, that a majority of the members appointed to the board of grain commissioners should be farmers actively engaged in agriculture. We believe that in the appointments made to that body more serious consideration should be given to the recommendations of the organizations that are particularly agricultural in their scope and purpose. We believe that in appointments to a board such as this every consideration should be given to the recommendations of such bodies as the wheat pool, which in this case placed before the government three names, which I believe was a proper course.
The choice was left to the government by providing an alternative. The farmers' union, representative as it is of many farmers in western Canada, gave its recommendation. The United Grain Growers gave its recommendation, and that is the one that was accepted by the government. We believe that the board of grain commissioners should be representative not only of the working farmer but also of organized agriculture. In these circumstances, and having placed the general view of the opposition before the house, it is our intention, in order to register our objection to this type of appointment, to oppose this bill in its present form. No other way is open to an opposition to register its opposition to what we object to, and the particulars of which we gave at the resolution stage. There is no other way in which

we can bifurcate our feelings by our vote. This, as we see it, represents an endeavour by the government to achieve a desirable end by adding to the bill, in the achievement of that end, features to which we strongly object. Having made the position clear, I again say that we object and will continue to object to the government following the course of introducing, holus-bolus, measures containing desirable features and at the same time, under the guise of doing that, bringing in features to which we object and to which we have no other means of objecting than by opposition.

Dear Mr. Howe:

Secretary,

My hon. friend will agonize less after knowing that.
This bill proposes to amend the Canada Grain Act in a number of respects. Section 1 of the bill provides that the salary of the chief commissioner of the board of grain commissioners shall be increased from $14,000 to $15,000 and the salaries of each of the two commissioners shall be increased from $12,000 to $13,500. The present salaries were established by an amendment to the Canada Grain Act in 1952. This amendment will bring the salaries into line with those which are being paid to persons carrying out comparable responsibilities in government and in private service.
Section 2 of the bill provides that an additional assistant commissioner shall be appointed so that there will be two for the province of Saskatchewan instead of the present one. Alberta and Manitoba will continue to have one each. The duties of the assistant commissioners generally fall into two main categories: they investigate specific complaints about infringements of the Canada Grain Act and they inspect country elevators to ensure that the equipment and records are in good order. The necessity for the appointment of an additional assistant commissioner in Saskatchewan is clear. Over one-half of all licensed country elevators in western Canada are located in Saskatchewan, namely 2,962 out of 5,356. Saskatchewan wheat production represents over half the total western wheat production. In the past ten years the average Saskatchewan wheat production has been 247 million bushels out of a prairie average of 418 million bushels.
Sections 3 and 4 of the bill give substantial implementation to a recommendation which was contained in the second report of the standing committee on agriculture and colonization during the last session of parliament. The report was dated June 2, 1954. In that report the committee recommended that terminal excess or overage which, under sections 139 and 140 of the Canada Grain Act, now becomes the property of Her Majesty should instead become the property of the Canadian wheat board. The proposed amendment will have that effect.
The committee further recommended that the value of such excess or overage should then be placed by the wheat board in the separate account provided in section 29A of the Canadian Wheat Board Act. This portion of the recommendation was given careful consideration but the opinion of the government is that the procedure outlined in the present amendment would be more flexible and more desirable. The objection to earmarking the money for section 29A is that
Canada Grain Act
it can then never be used in any other way by the wheat board and, of course, would not get back to the producers. Under the proposed amendment the funds could, if desirable, be placed under section 29A but at other times if more advantageous could be used to help defray the general expenses of the board and thus leave more money available for interim or final payments to producers.
Sections 5 and 6 of the bill amend the schedules to the act in so far as they refer to No. 3 Canada western and No. 3 Canada eastern amber durum wheat and all grades of soybeans. These amendments were recommended by the committees on western and eastern grain standards. These committees have representatives of the farmers, of the government and of the trade.
In the case of amber durum wheat, the amendment will make No. 3 amber durum a much more attractive proposition to overseas buyers. As hon. members know, durum wheat is used principally for the manufacture of macaroni. Certain varieties are better than others for this purpose. The amendment will ensure that the less desirable varieties may be graded no higher than No. 4. This is of great importance. In the past few years, because of growing conditions, a very high percentage of western durum wheat has been graded No. 3. In 1953-54, 3,686 cars graded No. 3 out of total durum inspections of 4,420 cars. Mainly this was because of growing conditions, but importers were reluctant to buy the grade because of the fact that it could contain the inferior varieties such as Pellisier and Golden Ball.
If the amendment is enacted, and if much of the crop again grades No. 3 because of growing conditions, there will not be the same reluctance on the part of overseas macaroni manufacturers. Pellisier and Golden Ball will of course continue to be grown by some producers because of their suitability to growing conditions in certain districts. These varieties will, however, be graded no higher than No. 4. They will still be used for other purposes such as puffed wheat, but they will no longer complicate the special requirements which exist for macaroni-making.
In the case of soybeans, it is gratifying to report that Canadian soybeans are being exported for the first time in history. Prior to the 1953 crop, there is no record of any export of Canadian soybeans. From October, 1953, to May, 1954, 568,000 bushels were shipped mainly to the United Kingdom. From the 1954 crop to the end of December, 595,282 bushels had been exported, again mainly to the United Kingdom. Prospects appear to be excellent since there seems to be

Canada Grain Act
a preference for the Canadian bean on a quality basis. The new-found export market, however, necessitates a clearer definition of the grading factors. The amended tables show maximum limits of damage and admixtures broken down into additional specific categories. The grades are thereby described more accurately than in the present schedule.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we in this group again strongly protest the circumstances surrounding the appointment of Mr. Loptson as a commissioner of the board of grain commissioners. We have heard an excerpt from a letter written by Mrs. Norman of the Saskatchewan farmers' union, and although I have not seen the whole text of the letter and have heard only the excerpt the minister read-

Excuse me, we have heard the whole letter. I am prepared to accept that if the minister says that is what he read. Apparently this represents the position of the Saskatchewan farmers' union. I would have been glad if he could have informed the house whether or not it was a decision of the executive of the Saskatchewan farmers' union.
I say to the minister he would be in a much better position as far as ascertaining for himself what the desires are of the farmers' union if he had obtained from them a recommendation supporting the appointment before it was made, instead of bringing to this house a statement concerning an appointment that was already an accomplished fact. It is not too easy for farm organizations to go on record concerning the wisdom or otherwise of an appointment after the appointment has been made, particularly when there are several appointments to the same board that are likely to come up and particularly when that organization, in the normal course of events, will have to deal with the board of grain commissioners many times in the future.
As far as I am concerned, I certainly strenuously object to the circumstances surrounding that appointment and more particularly to the information the minister gave to the house when we were considering it at the resolution stage.
I am wondering if the Saskatchewan wheat pool has made any comment, pro or con, since the appointment was made. We were told last year in excellent evidence given by a very competent witness, Mr. J. H. Wesson, the president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, when he appeared before the agriculture committee, that the Saskatchewan wheat
[Mr. Howe (Port Arthur) .1
pool has over 100,000 farmer members in that province. This is more than twice the number of members the U.G.G. has in all three of the western provinces combined.
If the minister had to choose one of three directors recommended by the Saskatchewan wheat pool, which is the large and representative grain handling farm organization in Saskatchewan and includes in its membership the vast majority of farm producers, there is no question but that he should have accepted the recommendations of the wheat pool in preference to the recommendations of the U.G.G.
If one wishes to compare the elevator systems in the province of Saskatchewan which are being managed by each of these companies, and if one compares the history of the companies and their sizes, there could be no doubt in the mind of a person who understands Saskatchewan that it is the Saskatchewan wheat pool which represents the voice of the wheat producers in relation to the marketing of grain. In view of this, I am amazed that the minister should turn down a recommendation presented by the Saskatchewan wheat pool. I was further astounded to hear the minister claim that he selected the most competent person. I believe that the directors of the Saskatchewan wheat pool are the people who are best acquainted with the farmers' position and the farmers' rights in the matter of grain handling. This is true because of the long experience the directors of the Saskatchewan wheat pool have had in the handling and marketing of grain and because of the fact that they manage the largest farmer-owned elevator system in the world.
The Saskatchewan wheat pool operates an elevator or elevators in almost every siding, village, city and town in the province of Saskatchewan. It consists of some 1,100 elevators which it has owned and operated for a great many years. As recently as 1948 the U.G.G. operated in the province of Saskatchewan just 100 elevators, and I am not at all certain that this figure did not represent the total number of elevators in their entire system. Later they bought another 125 line elevator houses. Why? The minister knows why. The reason is that the farmers decided to patronize their own system. And an additional 29 elevators were built. On the basis of the number of country elevators operated by these two companies the Saskatchewan wheat pool is four times as large an elevator system as the U.G.G. Despite this, the minister says that the director of the U.G.G. is in his opinion the most competent man of the group he had to choose from.

The minister went on to say that he caused a thorough investigation to be made of these people. He said this:
Each of the five men was very carefully investigated. I had reports on all of them from people whom I consider to be reliable witnesses.
I should like to know something about those inquiries and those reports. I should like to know who was doing the inquiring.
I venture to say that the people doing the inquiring probably did not know as much about the grain business as did the people they were inquiring about. I should like to know the names. The information is going to be brought out in a return but we should have it now instead of having to wait.
I should like to know the names of the directors of the Saskatchewan wheat pool elevator system that were recommended to the minister. I am wondering if it was the first vice-president at the time, Wes Ball, an extremely able and competent person. So able and competent is he that he was Canadian representative to the international federation of agricultural producers last year; so competent is he that recently he transferred his duties in the wheat pool organization as first vice-president to general manager of the country elevator system. I do not suppose there is any more directly responsible position in the grain business in Canada, as far as controlling actual operations is concerned, than is the position that Mr. Wes Ball now occupies. I am wondering whether he was one that was recommended as a candidate for the position. I am wondering whether Tom Beaubier, the second vicepresident, might have been a man that was recommended. He is another extremely competent person, who is now first vice-president of the wheat pool elevator system. He just recently stepped up from second vice-president to first vice-president. I am wondering whether they might have had the name of a young, able Saskatchewan farmer by the name of Charlie Gibbings.

The minister said a week ago- and as has already been referred to, it is a strange coincidence-that after the minister had made his mental decision as to the selection, between the time the mental decision was made and the decision itself-putting his name on the order or whatever a cabinet minister does when he appoints a man-there was brought to his attention the connection of this man with certain other people in the province of Saskatchewan. I did not put it forward as a fact at the time, but a week ago I said that I would not be surprised if the gentleman in question was on the Liberal executive in the constituency of the Minister of Agriculture. The Minister of Agriculture made no comment.
I do not like the way in which this appointment has been made. I hope the policy will be changed in the future. I hope that the farmers' main organizations will be given consideration in the appointments that are made. We want a board of grain commissioners that is manned by competent personnel. We want the personnel of the board of grain commissioners to be men who have the confidence of the producer and of organized agriculture. I can conceive of no suggestions as to personnel who might be more competent and have the confidence of the producer to any greater extent than would be the case if the government would put on the board of grain commissioners farmers belonging to

Canada Grain Act
farm organizations and farmers who have the confidence of the great body of organized agriculture in western Canada.
The hon. member for Prince Albert announced that he was voting against the bill. We know that this is another one of these package deals. In it there are some provisions that are a step in the right direction, and ones that we have recommended at various times in the past. We are glad to see that the government is now following them through. For example, one is that overages at the head of the lakes shall be turned in to the Canadian wheat board's funds instead of into the national treasury. I should like to have the clause worded somewhat differently. I should like to see these funds, when they become the property of the wheat board, disposed of by the wheat board not just on a recommendation from the governor general in council but on a recommendation from the farm organizations. These moneys belong to the producers. They cannot belong to anybody else. The producer has a just claim on them. The producers organizations themselves should be making the recommendations.
I should like to see this whole bill referred to the agriculture committee for study. I believe the agriculture committee should be called together and should have this bill presented before it. I believe that we should have the farm organizations appear before that committee and that we should find out not only what their comment is on the provisions of the bill itself but whether or not other amendments to the Canada Grain Act should not, in fact, now be made. I am thinking of amendments to the Canada Grain Act not only for western producers but of amendments to the Canada Grain Act that should be made in the interests of agriculture outside the prairie provinces, and in the interests of the feeders in the other seven provinces in Canada.

should be called before the committee. As I have said, we object to the circumstances surrounding the appointment of the new commissioner. We object to the increase in salaries. It is not an argument that registers with me particularly because I think you can find any number of competent men in western Canada who would be prepared to serve conscientiously and ably at the former salary. Certainly we object to any salary increases when there is no good evidence that the government has decided that the personnel of the board of grain commissioners shall have the full confidence of the farmers through being appointed on the recommendation of organized agriculture in the west. Because we object to this particular feature of the bill and because we would like some further inquiry into the Canada Grain Act and other matters set forth in the bill, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson):

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is necessary for me to add very much to what I said at the resolution stage. I pointed out then that there had been a great deal of criticism in western Canada of the operation of the Canada Grain Act, and that there was a good deal of discontent about the way the board of grain commissioners was operated. I also pointed out that practically all farm organizations were very high in their praise of the operation of the wheat board and that therefore I did not think it could be sajd the farm organizations would criticize simply for the sake of criticizing. When they find that a board is operating well they praise it, and when they find a board is not operating in the way they think it should operate they do not hesitate to criticize.
We were very glad to hear the minister state that the government had sought the advice of the various farm organizations in the appointment of another assistant commissioner, but I am sorry that the minister has not found it possible to accept their advice in that appointment. I do not know the gentleman mentioned, but I have listened to

Canada Grain Act
a lot of criticism of him. I hope that time will prove the minister was wise in making the appointment and that the gentleman will prove to be a good commissioner. I think time alone will show that. On the other hand, the minister would have saved himself a tremendous amount of criticism if he could have accepted the advice of the farm organizations when they offered it to him, but apparently he did not do that. So far as the provisions of the bill are concerned, we are in favour of them because the most contentious ones are measures that have been recommended by the various farm organizations. It seems to me that the criticism that has been made by former speakers is not so much of the bill but rather of the appointment made under the bill, that is the appointment of a commissioner. The bill merely makes provision for the appointment of an additional assistant commissioner. The bill itself does not make the appointment. It seems, therefore, the criticism is really being launched at the wrong point.
On the other hand, I am quite in accord with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) that the bill should be referred to the committee, because there are one or two things that I feel could be straightened out. I refer especially to the question of feed grain shipped east to Ontario. Every time I have been on an agriculture committee we have heard a lot of criticism from eastern members, not western members, of the type of grain they get under a certain grade. The minister says the grain is all bought under grade from the wheat board, and that is true. But the eastern buyers who buy that grain at grade are not compelled to sell it at the same grade; that is the criticism. The criticism is that these dealers buy grain under a certain grade, mix a lot of the other grain with it, and sell it at the same price although the grade has gone down. I am not making that charge, but I say that is the charge that has been levelled time and again by a number of witnesses who appeared before the committee.
I believe the farmers in the east are entitled to the protection that can be afforded to them by making feed agents sell the grain to the farmers at the grade laid down by the Canada Grain Act. They should not be allowed to dilute it. I feel that is a matter that could well be discussed by the agriculture committee.
Then, on the question of overages, we are glad to see the provision that the proceeds from the sale of overages will be turned over to the wheat board instead of the general revenue fund. We would like to see the government go a step farther and say that the

proceeds from the sale of all overages held by country elevators shall be also turned over to the wheat board. I cannot see how the proceeds from these overages belong to the country elevators. These country elevators today are merely acting as agents for the wheat board. Therefore, if there are any overages, which only accrue as a result of perhaps underweighing, the proceeds from them should be turned over to the wheat board.
In so far as salaries are concerned, I think it is in the interests of the farmers that we get the very best when we can for these jobs. It is necessary that whatever the salaries are, they be in line with the salaries for similar jobs in other concerns, otherwise we will not be able to get the type of men we should get. This makes it all the more necessary that the commissioners who are appointed should be men who have the confidence of the farmers in the country.
I think that is about all I need to say at this time. We feel it is probably a good thing to refer the subject matter of this bill to the agriculture committee in order that the committee may deal with the two points especially, the question of overages and the question of feed grains shipped to eastern Canada.

On that point, Mr. Speaker, I think probably it would be up to the government itself. This bill could easily go to the standing committee on agriculture, be dealt with there and the recommendations of that committee brought back to the house and dealt with at this session. I, too, want to support the idea that the subject matter should be sent to the committee for further study, and particularly the committee should study the matter of feed and screenings which are sent out under the authority of the board of grain commissioners. These screenings are bought by dealers in Ontario.
I happen to have here a certificate which came along with the bill of lading on a car shipped from Port Arthur on February 9, 1955, to a dealer in Ontario. The certificate of the board of grain commissioners states

that this is No. 1 feed screenings, the composition if which is given as 97 per cent broken grain and wild buckwheat, 2 per cent ball mustard and 1 per cent small seeds and chaff. I happened to see a sample of this material which was brought here by the hon. member for Wellington-Huron. In looking over the sample we found a considerable amount of that 97 per cent to be wild buckwheat and mustard. He said that quite frequently they got as high as 30 per cent or 40 per cent broken grain, and that made pretty fair feed, but the samples are getting worse. This sample was 95 per cent buckwheat and 1 per cent broken grain. By using the board of grain commissioners' definition of the composition of this, it is possible to ship out buckwheat, which is nothing but screenings. No definition covers it, and there should be a proper coverage of it. There should be a definition of the kind of feed screenings and the percentages. If you put the whole thing under the 97 per cent, including the buckwheat and the broken grain, that grain company can work in whatever it likes.

Did my hon.
friend ever hear screenings referred to as grain?

He bought it, as certified by your own board of grain commissioners, as No. 1 feed screenings. That is their definition, and it allows all the latitude up to 97 per cent of broken grain. If there is a sufficient quantity of broken grain in it, then you have pretty fair feed. If you get 3 per cent or 4 per cent broken grain and the rest wild buckwheat, and have to pay $1.65 per bushel for it, then it is no wonder the farmers in Ontario have complaints against the board.
The screenings are nothing more than dockage that has been removed from a man's grain. The farmer who ships in the grain gets paid nothing whatever for this dockage which is shipped out in the form of screenings and there is no control over it. This would be one method of straightening out that kind of thing, which is one of the causes behind the complaints that comes from farmers in Ontario who buy feed to feed their stock. This is the kind of thing that has been happening over and over again, and is one of the reasons why I would support the subject matter being referred to the committee. Let us have the representatives of
Canada Grain Act
the wheat pools before the committee because the board of grain commissioners could have a great deal of influence in cleaning up the whole matter and restoring the confidence of the growers and their organizations in the west as well as the farmers in the east.
The struggle between the private line elevator companies, the Winnipeg grain exchange and the pools is still continuing. They are fighting for the control of the grain in this country. You destroy confidence in the pools in the west when you take the president of the Winnipeg grain exchange and put him in control where he can practically wipe out the business of the pools. If we are going to maintain confidence in the operation of this important government institution, then some changes should be made. The confidence of the growers in the pools in the west should be maintained.

When I spoke a week ago I spent some time referring to the political activities of Mr. Allan McLean, who is in the pay of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It is significant that neither the Minister of Trade and Commerce nor the Minister of Agriculture made any reference to my remarks, but I want to stress again that

Canada Grain Act
western farmers, who find it so difficult these days to make ends meet, do not appreciate having men in positions of this kind with the background Mr. McLean has.
A week ago I referred to sessional paper 160. At that time I did not make it quite clear that Mr. McLean was not acting as national organizer of the Liberal party at the same time as he was being paid as one of the assistant grain commissioners. I wish to make it clear now that Mr. McLean was not doing both jobs. But when a person is as well known as that gentleman and goes to Melfort or Humboldt or Kelvington or Assiniboia or Swift Current, or any of the other places Mr. McLean visited between the time he gave up this job as national organizer of the party and the time immediately preceding the election of 1949, the farmers in that area have some trouble knowing whether he is visiting the area in the capacity of organizer of the party or as an employee of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I submit the government should be careful when making these obviously political appointments at salaries of this kind. And another point which I think must be considered carefully is the increasing of salaries of these men at this particular time. We see that the salary of the chief commissioner is being increased from $14,000 to $15,000, and those of the other commissioners from $12,000 to $13,500. These men are being paid out of the production of the farmers. Last year most of the farmers in my area received less than $1 a bushel for their wheat. And so the chief commissioner wants 15,000 bushels of wheat, clear, for his contribution to solving the problems of the farmers, while the other commissioners want 13,500 bushels of wheat delivered to the elevators on their account.
With the farmers finding it so difficult to have even enough to pay their taxes and other operating expenses, it becomes very difficult to explain to them why these very high salaries must be paid. I noticed in the last report of the board of grain commissioners the complaints do not indicate that the members of the board had an impossible task, or a task which could not have been done without an increase in their numbers. It appears that in the year ending December 31, 1953, there were 148 country complaints investigated and 141 in the preceding year. It seems to me that 148 complaints in the three prairie provinces does not represent a great deal of work.
To do this job there is a chairman, two commissioners and three assistant commissioners. It seems to me that these highly

paid men should be able to handle these complaints and other matters referred to the board without its becoming necessary to appoint another assistant commissioner. I feel sure that if these problems were referred to the committee on agriculture the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Agriculture and officials from both departments along with hon. members could present facts and figures which thus far have not been brought to the attention of the house. I feel sure hon. members would be well advised to accept the recommendation of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) to have this question referred to the committee on agriculture.

speechtext:
Clause 2 deals with an amendment to the act to enable the governor to appoint four assistant commissioners instead of three as at present. One of the assistant grain commissioners shall have headquarters in the province of Alberta, two in the province of Saskatchewan, and one in the province of Manitoba.
I think probably that is all to the good. The work they will have to do will doubtless keep them extremely busy. In fact, the vacancy among the assistant commissioners has led to a concentration of work on the part of those who are left to carry it on, and they have been somewhat unable to cope with all the problems facing them. A large number of inspections have to be made each year. The terminal elevators have to be weighed-over and complaints at storage elevators and line elevators have to be investigated. The work of the assistant grain commissioners is extremely onerous and will require full time if it is to be effective.
Since it has now been decided by this house that this bill is not to be referred to the committee on agriculture for further study, I feel we must urge the government to take action which will restore confidence among the grain growers in western Canada in this board. The way in which the board handles grain affects growers to an extent that is not readily understood by one who does not live in the west. Wheat pools have found their ability to handle grain completely stifled and curtailed, in my province to the extent of about 70 per cent, by members of this board either in their capacity as members of the board of grain commissioners or as transport controllers. The pools have found their handling of grain has been severely curtailed and cramped, and more and more grain is going back into the hands of the line companies. It is therefore my intention to move with regard to clause 2, seconded by the hon. member for Dauphin:
That section 2 of this bill be amended by adding at the end thereof, the following:
Section 5 of the said act is further amended by adding thereto the following additional subsection;
(4) Hereafter, all assistant grain commissioners shall be appointed on the recommendation of the three western wheat pools, and the interprovincial farm union council.
The purpose of that motion is to ensure that hereafter all assistant grain commissioners shall be appointed on the recommendation

Canada Grain Act
of the western wheat pools and the interprovincial farm union council, which is an organization with offices and representatives in both the west and the east. This will ensure that the interests of these organizations are being looked after to an extent which is not possible today. Certainly there is no evidence at the present time that their interests are being looked after in the best possible way. I therefore move the amendment to this clause.

speechtext: I wonder if the minister would care to comment on the suggestion that the members of this board should be appointed on the recommendation of the farm organizations? We are unable to move in committee that such a recommendation be followed in relation to the commissioners themselves because that section of the act is not before the committee, but we do suggest that this amendment to the clause be added in order to provide that the appointments will be made on the recommendation of the farm organizations. What my hon. friends really want is the right to make the appointment by the C.C.F, party in this house, and failing that they would accept the provision that men be appointed through certified C.C.F. voters. However, we cannot do that. There is a form of responsible government in this house that provides that those who are paid from the consolidated revenue fund are appointed by the governor in council of the day. We obtain our information as carefully as we can do so. In this case it would be my duty to make the recommendation, and I would expect to recommend a man I believed to be fully qualified for the job.
I am much interested to note that in framing this amendment providing for consultation with representative farmers' organizations in the country, no mention was made of the United Grain Growers. That is an old organization dating back, I think, to 1902. We have drawn three members from the wheat pool for the Canadian wheat board. I do not think we are overlooking the wheat pool but I do not know that there is any law of the land that requires every western appointment to be made on the recommendation of the Canadian wheat pools.
However, that is by the way. As I say, the method of governing this country requires that the governor in council take responsibility for all appointments to positions paid from
[Mr. Castleden.l
the consolidated revenue fund. We carry out the provisions of the constitution and obtain our recommendations from sources in which we have confidence.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am amazed at this debate on an amendment to this section of this bill. To me it means only one thing. In substance, from the beginning it is a denial of governmental responsibility for making any appointments.
However, I want to say two other things. I was one of the people who took some small part in the organization of the wheat pools in western Canada. They handle today in the neighbourhood of from 50 to 60 per cent of the grain of western Canada, and it is likely that their handling will increase. This suggestion is that a man be selected of their choice to administer this part of the Canada Grain Act. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, in all fairness, what the other 40 or 45 per cent of the trade would feel with that sort of appointment.
I come to our own province of Manitoba, and I look at the men who have been appointed as assistant commissioners in our province. This resolution, if passed, would deny the selection of the type of men who I think have been acceptable in the past in Manitoba. I refer first of all to Dr. T. J. Harrison who was for a long time head of our agronomy department at the University of Manitoba. He in turn was followed by the appointment of Mr. Rayner, the secretary of the board, who acted in that capacity for some time. The latest appointment is another agriculture graduate who was associated with the department of agriculture in our province for a number of years.
I do not know where you could find a more impartial, acceptable type of men with a good scientific agricultural background for carrying out their duties under this act. For my part I just cannot accept the idea that you are going to designate the type of men to be selected by a certain organization to fill these appointments, even if they are associated with the pools, which no doubt have a good deal of influence in western Canada. I just cannot see that that is a reasonable proposition, when they have to deal particularly with pool people and non-pool people as well.

I leave it to the consideration of the committee whether it is logical to select for a field job under this act a man well grounded in scientific agriculture, who can not only administer the act but can give a good deal of inspiration and leadership with respect to the production of good seeds and things of that kind which are essential all over western Canada, and especially in the province of Manitoba. That type of appointment has met with the approval of both the private trade and the pools, and I think it will continue to do so.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO WATER POLLUTION
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 186, to amend the Criminal Code (nuisance).
He said: In rising to move second reading of this bill, Mr. Speaker, I would point out simply the purpose and aim I have in mind in asking for an amendment to the Criminal Code. You will notice from a reading of the bill, sir, that it has to do with interprovincial rivers. Perhaps I should read part of the bill in order to discuss it. The section reads:
Every owner, lessee, or person operating any industrial plant, oil refinery, chemical works, sawmill or other plant or works, or any other person, who discharges or throws or allows to be discharged or thrown any noxious waste product raw sewage, oil, sawdust, chemical or other matter or thing into a river, stream or other water any part of which is interprovincial or which flows into any interprovincial water, which has the effect of endangering the lives, safety, health or comfort of the public is guilty of
(a)	an indictable offence and is liable to a fine of ten thousand dollars for a first offence and of twenty thousand dollars for a second offence, or
(b)	an offence punishable on summary conviction.
Criminal Code
Under those circumstances, if summary conviction proceedings were taken the penalty would be fixed by the statute which comes into effect on April 1, provided the bill before us today becomes law and receives royal assent. I should like to point out, too, that there is a section in the Criminal Code at the present time covering the commission of a nuisance. The material section, as I see it, states:
A common nuisance is an unlawful act or omission to discharge a legal duty, which act or omission endangers the lives, safety, health, property or comfort of the public, or by which the public are obstructed in the exercise or enjoyment of any right common to all His Majesty's subjects.
The variation of that would be "Her Majesty's subjects". However, that section in its present form would not, as I see it, permit the prosecution of anyone who pollutes the rivers of this country, whether they be interprovincial or otherwise. The purpose of the amendment is to effectively control under the criminal law the dumping of contaminants into interprovincial rivers, a practice which has turned several of Canada's rivers into veritable running sewers and cesspools.
When I say that, I could give various examples of rivers that are not interprovincial. However, I am restricting the application of the section I have in mind to interprovincial rivers the water supply of which is being wantonly polluted by industrial concerns or municipalities, thereby constituting a gross and needless denial of the right of the public to the water supply with which nature has so richly provided our country.
The first time this matter came before the house for discussion was about a year ago, when people in Saskatchewan and Manitoba resident on the North Saskatchewan river found themselves denied the use of the waters of this great river by reason of pollution, mainly by an industrial concern which carries on business some miles east of the city of Edmonton. In Prince Albert, a city of some 20,000 population, in Battleford and also in The Pas in Manitoba, people along this river were denied the use of its waters. No one who was not in one of those cities or towns during the months of December, 1953, January, February and March of 1954 has any idea of the extent to which contamination rendered those waters unusable.
This is not a problem peculiar to our country. It is one which exercises the minds of various people in the United States. In that country the criminal law is under the jurisdiction of the several states, and for that reason a major portion of the responsibility for meeting the problem of pollution rests

Criminal Code
upon those states, which alone possess the police powers necessary to punish any invasion of the rights of individuals in this connection. This problem has been intensified in the last 50 years and there is a pronounced interest, not only in our own country but also in the United States, respecting surveys of water resources and the correction of waste discharges which go with an expanding economy and the continually accelerating industrial development.
I should like to quote from the Industrial and Engineering Chemistry magazine concerning the problem in the United States. It states:
In many areas these wastes have interfered with the comforts and recreational pursuits of the public. All too frequently surface and underground water supplies have been damaged, sometimes irreparably. Nature has provided means for the self-purification of waterways, but these are often inadequate for coping with wastes from great urban areas or heavy industrial concentrations. In these circumstances man must devise supplemental methods for lightening the pollution loads entering the streams to amounts that can be stabilized by natural forces.
Seven years ago in the United States the federal water pollution control act was passed, the objects of which were as follows: to assist in pollution abatement work under the law; comprehensive program development; interstate co-operation; uniform state legislation; enforcement; reporting; financial assistance; research; and also participation in river basin development programs. Another object was the preservation and improvement of the quality of the nation's water resources. The purpose was to ensure an adequate present and future supply of water for all beneficial uses, for while our water supply has remained constant the number of water users has been increasing to an extent that could not have been imagined 50 years go. In 50 years industrialization along the waterways in the United States has increased by 700 per cent.
We find ourselves in the same position in Canada, and I would refer to the North Saskatchewan river merely as an example. With the chemical industrialization that is taking place in the city of Edmonton, unless action is taken by the provincial and federal governments we may well find ourselves in a few years in the position that the vast water resources of that river have been transformed into a cesspool, so the cities depending upon that water will no longer have it available. Besides this, a chemical industry developing at the present tim% in Alberta, and in the years ahead in Saskatchewan as our oil development expands, will require greater and greater quantities of water of especially high quality.

For these reasons I believe action must be taken, and the only body that can take action effectively on an interprovincial river is the parliament of Canada. Just take the example of the North Saskatchewan river. So long as the pollution takes place at a point east of Edmonton, in Alberta, very little harm is done to the people in that province. However, the water taking some 30 days to travel from Edmonton to Prince Albert, people in cities like Prince Albert and Battleford, and again in Manitoba down to The Pas are left in a position where their respective provincial governments can do nothing to protect them from the actions of industrial concerns or municipalities in another province.
In the United States this was viewed first as a national problem and secondly, for pollution purposes, as a state problem. They brought about not only co-operation between federal and state governments, but through the activities of the federal government they were able to secure industrial co-operation.
I want to be fair in this matter. The Canadian Chemical Company Limited was largely responsible for the pollution that took place in the North Saskatchewan river last year, and again recently for a week or ten days. That corporation has devoted itself to removing the danger of pollution in large measure by the dumping of chemical effluents into the river. But there is nothing to prevent any corporation or, indeed, any cities located in Alberta from polluting that stream without regard to the rights of residents in Saskatchewan and Manitoba.
Facing a similar situation in the United States the federal government co-operated with the states, whereby ten interstate compacts were entered into including pollution abatement in their objectives, to prevent unnecessary pollution by agreement and by the implementation of comprehensive plans. What I have before me is a summary of the legislation in the United States in this connection.
Having said that, I want to refer to what has happened in other parts of Canada within the last few months. The anti-pollution league of the province of Quebec has given the fullest consideration to the pollution of the Ottawa river. I am not giving that as an example of an interprovincial river; I am simply referring to the findings of this league, which are to the effect that unless effective action is taken the Ottawa river, one of the great rivers of Canada, will establish within itself the chemical and bacteriological characteristics of a sewer in action. This river was examined in detail by the league, and their conclusions are as follows:
The results that have been delivered and commented are, we believe, decisive enough for the

conclusions arising from them to be immediately obvious. The Ottawa river in the sectors extending from Ottawa-Hull to Thurso-Plaisance and from Hawkesbury-Grenville as far as Carillon is heavily polluted by industrial waste matters and heavily contaminated by municipal sewage; the water is dangerous and its use for industrial purposes is already impaired.
It finally concludes that under the laws as they now exist there is not that control which is necessary for the preservation of this vast resource. The province of Ontario in 1953 set up a pollution control board, the objective being to raise the water quality so as to satisfy the requirements of the various departments that have participated in forming the board.
However, so far as an interprovincial river is concerned, as the law is at present nothing can be achieved except where the provinces affected operate jointly to the end that the causes of pollution be removed. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) attended a conference held in Regina last fall which was attended by representatives of the three western provinces. Saskatchewan submitted a brief which I believe summarizes the situation in fairly complete and succinct form, when they say:
In the opinion of the government of Saskatchewan any plan to solve the problem of water pollution, in so far as it affects the public health, should take into consideration the following points:
(1)	Any plan should include control of surface and ground waters.
(2)	The plan should be sufficiently flexible to provide for varying circumstances and needs. If water is required for industrial or other use it would be expected that such use would be considered with due regard to the problems of the health of domestic water users.
(3)	Provision should be made for a complete survey of the present status of the water resources with particular emphasis on the source and extent of pollution. A continuing check on existing and new sources of pollution should be provided for.
(4)	Provision should be made for adequate facilities being available to study the human toxicological biological effects of the various polluting elements.
These were the objectives. Then the government of Saskatchewan went on to suggest a means by which they could be achieved. The brief says that the matter of interprovincial streams is more difficult than that of provincial streams. The final conclusion in this brief was that a joint board on river pollution control should be set up, representative of the three provinces concerned as well as of the dominion government. It went on to say:
The joint board should have an executive officer who preferably would be a competent engineer and who would have authority to call upon the technical consultative services of appropriate agencies in the various provinces.
The joint board would not be assumed to have direct control or administrative functions . . .
Representations were made by various municipalities to the effect that in addition
Criminal Code
to the setting up of such a board, parliament had a responsibility which it could exercise only through the medium of an amendment or amendments to the Criminal Code. As far as the setting up of an interprovincial board is concerned, apparently the present position is that the government of Saskatchewan has come to the conclusion that the government of Alberta is not giving that co-operation which would be necessary for the board to achieve success. I quote from the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of November 3 last, summarizing the situation:
The prospect of a permanent and highly satisfactory solution to the problem of pollution in prairie rivers looked bright following the conference of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and federal government officials in Regina last month. But the statement released the other day by this province's minister of public health, Hon. T. J. Bentley, raises a number of doubts regarding Alberta's readiness to co-operate. The disturbing feature of Mr. Bentley's statement is his intimation that the Alberta government refuses to accept the proposal of the Regina conference for a full-time intergovernmental board with technical staff, preferring instead a committee without continuity or secretariat.
The article concludes by suggesting that federal action is necessary in order to meet the situation.
When I refer to what took place on the prairies, I am not asking for an amendment to the Criminal Code in order to cover the ad hoc situation in the three western provinces. The same situation prevails on other interprovincial rivers in Canada. As Dr. Lucien Piche, head of the University of Montreal, said: They are becoming unsuitable for any use whatsoever. His reference, of course, was to the Ottawa river; but it applies with equal force to other interprovincial rivers. The heading in the Montreal Gazette was: "Pollution makes the Ottawa river little better than an open sewer."
That is the potential situation on the North Saskatchewan river. The same could apply to the South Saskatchewan river, and to other rivers across the country. Last fall the Prime Minister was asked what the government intended to do. According to the press report in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix he communicated with the Battle-ford board of trade and advised in part as follows:
Reactions of Saskatchewan and Manitoba to the Alberta proposals are being awaited before further consideration to this matter is given by the federal government.
The position is that the province of Saskatchewan, within the limitation of its powers, brought a bill before the legislature to the following effect:
A person who deposits or causes or allows to be deposited along the bank of a running stream in

Criminal Code
Saskatchewan, or who casts or throws into its waters stable manure or night soil, carcasses, sawdust, salt water, any matter or form of industrial waste or other filthy or impure matter is guilty of an offence and liable . . .
-to the penalties provided therein. This amendment to the Saskatchewan statutes will not help solve the problem of the dumping of industrial wastes into the North Saskatchewan river in Alberta. That type of amendment will merely cover the situation within the province of Saskatchewan. If similar legislation were passed by Manitoba it would merely cover the situation within the province of Manitoba.
The Saskatchewan association of mayors and heads of municipalities has petitioned for an amendment to the Criminal Code to cover the situation. It is sometimes argued -the Minister of Justice advanced this argument last year-that interprovincial rivers are a matter of provincial legislative responsibility. The Criminal Code is designed, as I see it, in the nuisance section and in particular the section to which I refer, to cover actions similar to those which have resulted in the past in the denial to the people of urban centres of the use of the waters of the river which passes through their territorial limits. There is no power in any province to punish, and thereby prevent, the wrongdoing that takes place in another province. The present section of the Criminal Code merely covers unlawful acts or omissions. Both the act and the omission must be unlawful. There is nothing in the dumping into rivers of waste products of industrial concerns that would give any cause of action under that section.
The federal government accepts tlje responsibility under the Fisheries Act of punishing the wrongdoing of those who dump sawdust into rivers and thereby detrimentally affect or even cause the asphyxiation of fish. The dominion government accepts the responsibility of punishing under law anyone who dumps waste into navigable streams. But in regard to the health and comfort of human beings who depend on these streams for their water supply the attitude is taken that there is no right or responsibility in the federal authority to act within the provisions of the criminal law.
I find it difficult to understand why the dumping or throwing of sawdust, slabs, bark or rubbish into a navigable river is an offence when it is not an offence for municipalities or industrial concerns to use the waters of an interprovincial stream to free themselves of what they do not want, the effluent from their operations, by the simple expedient of throwing it into the river, and thus confer

that pollution and its effects upon others. I do not wish to say more at this time but I point out that there is no action that can be taken other than an amendment to the Criminal Code.
Last November the Prime Minister gave the board of trade to understand that unless the three western provinces could meet this problem in a spirit of co-operation the federal government would consider taking the only action that I think is possible under law to preserve and maintain these God-given sources of water, which are limited and which will be more and more needed as our industrialization expands. These selfish concerns, by the simple act of removing from themselves what they do not want, by dumping it into a moving stream, deny the use of that water to the people; and having disposed of the effluent they have no responsibility to maintain and preserve the right of others to the equal use of the waters of the streams.
The United States did not act in the national field until seven years ago, for the reason that the criminal law is the responsibility of the states. However, the United States found that in addition to the provisions of the criminal law in a number of states- and my recollection is that it is in operation in 13 states at the present time-there was also brought into being through federal cooperation the board to which I alluded at the beginning of my remarks.
I make the serious appeal to this house, not only on behalf of the people resident on the Saskatchewan rivers but on behalf of people resident on all interprovincial streams, that action be taken now which will enable the use of the power and authority of law to punish those who place their own convenience above the needs of the multitudes of people who are dependent upon the use of the waters of these streams which are polluted through the actions of those who give no consideration to others.
Last year when Prince Albert and other urban centres were as devoid of water as though they were situated on a desert, an aroused public opinion asked for and demanded action. A few weeks ago, for a period of about a week or ten days, a similar pollution took place which the company in question stated had arisen through the negligence of an employee. The fact that this corporation has acted recently and is doing its part to remove the probability of a repetition of this occurrence does not remove the need for action on that and other interprovincial rivers.

A reading of the summary of the legislation in the United States indicates that that country waited too long before acting, on both the state and federal levels. I ask that the house view this matter not in a partisan way but from the point of view of the people of this country. Our population is increasing, industrialization is being accelerated, and water supplies to all intents and purposes are unchanged. The location of urban centres on interprovincial rivers was no accident. It was the choice of those who first settled in those areas. They were eager to ensure that their water supply would continue not only during the course of their lives but for generations yet unborn.
Unless teeth are put in the criminal law which will punish those selfish persons who would deny the people of this country the use of the pure water that nature has rendered available, within a very few years we shall find that streams from which the people have a right to expect to draw supplies of pure water will be polluted and defiled and will in effect be in the condition of one river, which Professor Piche described as a floating sewer. Provincial governments cannot meet the situation. I submit that the criminal law was intended to cover offences against the people as a whole, and that anyone who wrongfully pollutes the interprovincial streams of our country thereby commits a crime not only against the present generation but against generations yet to come.
I ask the support of the hon. members of this house in bringing about an amendment that will give to the people of this country who live on interprovincial streams the authority to act not against those who on a single occasion might inadvertently pollute a stream in this country, but against those who make it a policy of selfishness, if you will, to pollute the streams in order to save themselves the trouble of bringing into being measures which they could establish to remove the dangers of pollution. They feel it is easier and less costly for them to rid themselves of the effluent they do not want by placing it in the streams, but as a result of their actions those in other provinces who have the right to the use of waters of the interprovincial streams are denied that right.
That, Mr. Speaker, in summary represents what I have in mind in introducing this amendment asked for by the association of municipalities to which I have made reference, and demanded by tens of thousands of people-literally hundreds of thousands-in this country who are asking for some action on the part of the federal government to protect them from the cupidity of those who, because of their power, believe they can with 50433-138
Criminal Code
impunity deny the use of these waters to present and future generations.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that no one will be in disagreement with the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) as to the importance of the issue which he has raised or as to his suggestion that it should not be approached as a partisan matter. Certainly I shall not approach it as such.
This is the second occasion in as many years on which we have discussed this issue and I must say that I have seen no reason to change the views which I expressed on a former occasion, in spite of the fact that notwithstanding what my hon. friend from Prince Albert has said, a great deal of progress has been made toward the solution of this problem. I should like to report to the house with regard to the conference which took place at Regina to which my friend the hon. member for Prince Albert has referred because, as I said in this chamber last year, I think an approach of that sort is much more effective than is the method which he is now recommending. Before doing that, however, I should like to make one or two observations with regard to his actual amendment itself.
If I understood him correctly-and I hope he will correct me if I have not done so- he stated that there is not in the code at the present time any section which could be invoked to deal with the sort of situation which arose in Prince Albert last year. If he looks at section 165 of the new Criminal Code which will come into effect on April 1-

Yes. My hon. friend is amending the new code but he is making his references to the nuisance sections of the present, or old, code. There is not a great deal of difference; but in order to keep the record uniform, I think I had better refer to the new code to which his present bill is submitted as an amendment. Under the heading of "nuisances", section 165 reads as follows:
165. (1) Every one who commits a common nuisance and thereby
(a)	endangers the lives, safety or health of the public, or
(b)	causes physical injury to any person,
is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years.
Then, as I am sure my hon. friend will agree, if it is a corporation which is convicted of that indictable offence, the fine will

Criminal Code
not be the limited fine which my hon. friend's amendment provides but will be a fine in the discretion of the court which under section 623 will be completely unlimited in amount. Then subsection 2 of section 165 reads as follows:
(2) For the purposes of this section every one commits a common nuisance who does an unlawful act or fails to discharge a legal duty and thereby
(a)	endangers the lives, safety, health, property or comfort of the public, or
(b)	obstructs the public in the exercise or enjoyment of any right that is common to all the subjects of Her Majesty in Canada.
Having regard to the fact that in the Alberta provincial law and in the federal Fisheries Act there are provisions that prohibit the discharge of effluents and the placing of waste in the Saskatchewan river in Alberta, everyone who by so doing commits an unlawful act in breach of these Alberta regulations or federal statutes and thereby endangers the lives, safety or health of the public, falls squarely within the present section 165.
