speechtext: That is exactly the point I make. The mere dumping of these effluents is not an unlawful act. Would the minister say what an unlawful act would be within the meaning of the section?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO WATER POLLUTION
speechtext:
An unlawful act is one which is done in contravention of the law. If my hon. friend wants to read it, he will find that section 33, subsection 2, of the Fisheries Act provides that no person shall cause or knowingly permit to pass into, or put or knowingly permit to be put, lime, chemical substances and so on into the waters of a river like the North Saskatchewan. That being the case, I would much prefer to place reliance upon the existing law than upon the amendment which has been moved by my hon. friend.
It will be observed that, amongst other defects of his amendment, he discriminates between public corporations like municipalities and private corporations which are the only ones which he names in his bill. That would mean that a municipality in Alberta could contaminate the river as much as it liked and would leave the people in Prince Alberta without recourse under his amendment.
But it would mean more than that. It would mean that if, instead of discharging its effluent directly into the river, an industrial corporation put it into the sewers of the city of Edmonton, it would not come under my hon. friend's bill. The moral blame

would be there, if you like, but there would be no legal consequence under his bill as drafted. If my hon. friend wishes to cover a case of that kind, he must make his bill applicable to municipalities; and if he makes it applicable to municipalities I think he will find that, apart from any protests that might arise from industry in Canada, not only in Saskatchewan and Alberta but in all the other provinces, he would create a situation which would be extremely mischievous indeed, if not oppressive upon many Canadian municipalities. The hon. member for Prince Albert says he is not seeking by his amendment to cover an ad hoc situation and deal merely with the North Saskatchewan river. He says the situation is so bad all over Canada, and he instanced at some length the Ottawa river, that something should be done along the lines of his amendment throughout Canada, but only in interprovincial rivers. It is a rather remarkable thing that, in spite of the bad situation to which he refers and which he says has been prevalent in the more industrialized sections of Canada for these many years, no municipalities or other public interests have asked to have passed any amendment like the one which he is now advocating.
I said last year and I repeat now that in my humble view, which I think is supported by the arguments of my hon. friends as to the way in which this matter was grappled with in the United States and the way in which it is being dealt with by the international joint commission in a very highly industrialized section of Canada opposite Detroit and other large industrial cities of that part of the United States, it is only by the concerted efforts of joint administrative boards that efforts can be put forth by chemists, sanitary engineers and those people whose knowledge equips them to deal with a problem of this sort. That was the method which I suggested in the house last year should be followed in the case of the North Saskatchewan river.
It was rather gratifying that the suggestion made in the debate in the house at that time was taken up by the province of Saskatchewan which called an interprovincial conference at Regina, to which the hon. member has referred. Premier Douglas of Saskatchewan suggested to the Prime Minister that the government of Canada should be represented at the interprovincial conference, and I had the honour to represent this government at that conference.
It was a very successful conference indeed. Representing the province of Saskatchewan were Premier Douglas, Hon. T. J. Bentley, minister of public health and minister in

charge of health services planning commission, Hon. L. F. McIntosh, minister of municipal affairs, Dr. F. B. Roth, deputy minister of health, Dr. M. S. Acker, director of research and statistics branch, department of health, Mr. Prescott of the sanitary engineering division, department of health, Mr. Scammell, member of the prairie provinces water board and of the engineering subcommittee of the international joint commission, and Dean F. C. Cronkite, dean of law, university of Saskatchewan.
Representing Alberta were Dr. A. Somerville, deputy minister of public health, and Mr. Bouthillier, of the University of Alberta. From Manitoba there were Hon. Frank C. Bell, minister of health and public welfare, Hon. C. E. Greenlay, minister of mines and natural resources and Mr. L. A. Kay, director of public health engineering, department of health and public welfare. Representing the government of Canada were D. H. W. Henry of the Department of Justice, Dr. K. C. Charron, Department of National Health and Welfare, and myself.
I have been at a good many conferences between governments in my time and I do not know of any at which, in my view, more satisfactory progress was made in a shorter period of time than at the conference at Regina. We began our work promptly at nine o'clock in the morning and by six o'clock that night we had reached a number of conclusions which it seemed to me, as one who is not particularly skilled in these scientific matters, were singularly intelligent and worth while. When it was over I made a draft statement as to what had taken place at the conference and I submitted it to all the provincial governments concerned so that in stating here what the positions taken at Regina were I would not be prejudicing them in any way. I have clearance from all of the governments that this is a correct statement of what took place at that conference.
The first thing was that at the opening of the proceedings I made it clear that I was attending pursuant to an undertaking which the Prime Minister had given to Premier Douglas that a member of the federal government would attend the conference and give such assistance as he could. At the conference it was unanimously agreed by all present that the three prairie provinces would join together in setting up a proposed joint pollution control board with functions as follows. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Clause 3 specifies, in effect, that all grain commonly known as overages that appears in public terminal elevators shall be confiscated by the board of grain commissioners, and the proceeds thereof shall be the property of the Canadian wheat board and shall be disposed of by that board as the governor in council directs.
I do not suppose anyone who is familiar with the grain business is foolish enough to

Canada Grain Act
believe you can handle several hundred million bushels of grain without having overages. I do feel, however, that these overages could be curtailed in a large measure provided the board of grain commissioners accepted their responsibility as laid down in the act.
While this bill only covers those overages which occur in public terminal elevators, I feel there is some question as to the validity of that statement. While I do not intend to dispute that here and now, I would say that we feel there are a great many more overages in public terminal elevators than would seem to be necessary.
We believe the board of grain commissioners should accept their responsibility to see they are kept to a minimum. The last financial statement issued by the board of grain commissioners covered the confiscation of overages, and showed that all the grain the board could find in terminal elevators amounted to some $289 and some odd cents. This does not indicate the large amount of grain that was taken in overages and not accounted for by the board of grain commissioners.
There are, of course, two or three factors which account for these overages. First of all there is the mixing of grain which, in effect, results in the grain being upgraded. You take dry grain and mix it with tough or damp grain, and you immediately have an upgrading of that grain.
Then, of course, there are the overages which occur because of the weighing itself. I believe one of the things in which the board of grain commissioners has fallen down rather badly, and which accounts for a tremendous number of bushels in overages, is the drying process. If we look at the figures for 1952-53, we find that according to the report of the Canadian wheat board they took in some 59 million bushels of tough or damp grain. They artificially dried a little over 2 million bushels of that, with the result that some 56 million odd bushels of grain were dried otherwise. A percentage of dry grain was used to mix with the tough and damp grain in order to bring the moisture content down to something that was acceptable. I feel that is one place where a large percentage of overages accrue.
In 1952-53 the Canadian wheat board had something over 2 million bushels of grain for which no producer certificates were issued. Our contention is that that 2 million bushels must have been overages; there was no other place for it to come from. In the report for last year we find there were 1,386,300

bushels for which no producer certificates were issued. We contend that this represents overages. As I said in the first instance, I believe a great part of these overages accrue because of the fact the grain is upgraded, as we call it, in the process of drying. Of course my remarks relate only to wheat, and we must take into consideration the tremendous number of bushels of barley, oats, and rye for which there is no account whatever.
It is the hope of the farmers of western Canada that the board of grain commissioners will make a thorough and exhaustive study of this question of grain overages. Certainly something should be done, and I feel the board of grain commissioners can no longer ignore the necessity for making a complete study of the whole question of overages. It is a contentious problem. In the meantime these overages do occur, and it is with the disposition of the money that accrues from the sale of these overages that this clause is concerned. I feel that actually the money belongs to the producers, and I am wondering about the administrative problem of getting that money into the hands of the producers according to the marketings they have made as individuals.
It is because of that I am moving, seconded by the hon. member for Kindersley:
That clause 3 be amended by deleting from line 28 all the words after the words "that board" and by substituting therefor the following words: "on the recommendation of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and interprovincial farm union council."

The assistance is paid under this act on the gold produced and sold to the Royal Canadian Mint by a mine in a calendar year. subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are now asked to give second reading to Bill No. 190, to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. The effect of this bill, as the minister acknowledged at page 1590 of Hansard, will be to reduce the amount of subsidy paid to the gold mining industry in Canada from an estimated $16 million in 1954 to an estimated $11 million in 1955 and 1956.
In this time of substantial unemployment, why should any government embark upon a restrictive policy toward an industry which employs directly over 18,800 men, and indirectly gives employment to many thousands more, when there is involved an industry the product of which is gold which is not capable of overproduction and is not in competition with private business?
Again, how can the government justify the loss of any gold to our gold reserves at a time when capital, which can and may be withdrawn, has been pouring into Canada? With $12 billion of foreign capital invested in Canada, $8 billion of which is repayable in United States dollars, can anyone say that our gold reserves of $1,072 million, or even our combined gold and United States dollars
2178	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act reserves, which are still under $2 billion- the latest figure is $1,942 million, at the end of the year-are sufficient, remembering always that these reserves have to meet our trade deficits as well as establish our monetary reserves behind our currency?
I admit that the place of gold in international finance is a controversial subject, particularly when governments in large sections of the world are totalitarian in form and communist in belief, and when much of the world has been beguiled by socialism. Nevertheless, it continues to be money in the freer parts of the world, and it continues to be the standard and anchor of value in all parts of the world for the simple reason that the United States dollar and gold bullion are interchangeable at $35 an ounce. Until I see someone who has the opportunity to refuse gold doing so, I think I am justified in assuming that gold still holds its historic place as currency and the standard of value.
I am reminded of the importance of gold as currency by an episode that concerned me when I was travelling as a student on the border of Austria and Switzerland. One of those combination immigration and customs officers with a clanking sword took me by the arm and began to speak to me in German, which I could not understand, by the way.
I realized that he was saying something about gold: "Haben sie etwas geld?" Gold was the only thing he was concerned about on my person. My exit from Austria depended on whether or not I had any gold in my pocket.
Why then should anyone think of subsidizing the production of the one substance which is the measure of value? It would be difficult to suggest a more nonsensical proposition in economics unless it would be to prescribe that all debts should be paid twice over, at least for the time being.
If gold cannot pay for its own recovery why should public funds be used to pay for it? Nevertheless that is exactly what this government decided to do as recently as eight years ago, and this house approved. It has approved from time to time and will approve again this year the subsidy on the mining of gold. If international financial arrangements have become so debevilled by war and postwar inflation, then this government which has a part, and has had a part, in making international monetary and trade agreements for 20 years now must take its full share of blame for the state of affairs which makes the subsidization of gold seem sensible and necessary.
In fairness I might add that even our government has to live not only with its own mistakes but with the mistakes of other governments, and it is therefore not entirely & free agent. In any event, in 1947 this


government found it necessary either to let the gold mines fade and the gold communities die, and forgo the production of gold or pay more for the gold being produced. Mr. Abbott announced his decision by radio on November 17, 1947. The house will remember that the international monetary fund agreement does not permit a member country to increase the price of gold except within the margins allowed, which were not applicable to this case; therefore that formula required modification, and in due course the Department of Finance devised a new and acceptable formula which the international monetary fund approved, which was based not on a direct subsidy to increase the price of gold per ounce but a subsidy based on the cost of production of gold per ounce. Then we had the first bill, which came into force on January 1, 1948, for a term of three years. The formula was one-half the current cost of producing gold in excess of $18 per ounce, applied to part only of the production of the mine.
We have had from the minister and his department a report on the results of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. I shall not take the time of the house to detail the experience under this legislation, which has been renewed from time to time and is still in force, but I would refer the house to schedule I on page 10, which shows the payments. It shows the number of mines operating in each of the years during which this assistance has been in effect from 1948 to 1953 inclusive, the amount of assistance paid, the number of ounces produced and the average price per ounce. With the permission of the house I should like to place the table on Hansard so it will appear in the record. It is not long. I have added to the table the estimated figures for 1954.

I think it is proper to suggest that the net cost is something else, because if all those mines paid income tax not only on the assistance but on other profits, estimated at from 60 to 75 per cent of the gold assistance, it would reduce the net cost by from $20 to $33 million for the seven year period, which is not a very large sum of money when one considers the results obtained.

Some $787 million worth of gold was produced in those seven years of subsidy. That is almost exactly the amount by which the gold reserves of this country have been increased in the same seven years, and is precisely 73 per cent of the present gold reserve. It is an interesting speculation as to what our gold reserve would be today had this assistance not been paid.
If the reasons which impelled parliament in 1947 to institute this subsidy were good, they are far better today than they were then. That is why I find it very difficult to understand the proposal made by the minister not to continue the subsidy in full, or on as good terms, but to reduce and restrict it by changing the formula with the avowed expectation that the subsidy will be cut by $5 million or 31 per cent of the subsidy which is being paid in the year 1954.
What is the view of the gold mines? I do not think they relish the idea of being a subsidized industry. Some of them frankly would prefer to close, because gold in the earth is not a wasting asset and can be mined when that can be done profitably. But there are other important considerations, the communities, the people involved in those mining towns, as well as the shareholders of the companies who number some hundreds of thousands of Canadians whose investments are in this form of security. Therefore they have very little choice in the matter but to mine as long as any profit can be made.
Their case this year, as compared with 1948, if they were advocating assistance, is much better statistically. Not only is the price they receive for gold today less than it was in 1947 because of the premium at which our dollar stands, and which results in a price of less than the $35 an ounce for gold which we would receive if the dollar were at par, but in addition the costs of mining have increased in the past few years.

I should like to indicate to the house exactly what the costs of mining are today. Taking 1940 as the base, the cost of gold mining has doubled since that date; and at the same time the value of the product which gold mines have to sell has depreciated by 12 per cent. If you offset these figures one against the other you can see the impossible position of the gold mining industry. Costs have doubled and there has been a reduction of 12 per cent in the selling price of the product gold, within the same period.
Now, excluding taxes, the average costs of Ontario gold mines, which I give as an illustration, have increased since 1940 by $12.12 per ounce of gold production. The price which has been received from the mint for gold has dropped from $38.50-that was the price when the Canadian dollar was at a discount of 10 per cent in 1940-to a price of $33.85 in December, 1954, and a corresponding price today depending on the exchange rate. This is an additional $4.65 per ounce of extra cost, or rather conversely, $4.65 of less return for each ounce of gold produced. So the total net reduction so far as the mine is concerned is $16.77 per ounce of gold produced. They are that much worse off.
The assistance in that period has been about $4.23 per ounce, which is just about 25 per cent of the reduction the mines have suffered in the period during which the assistance has been paid. The possible effect of the proposal which the minister now brings forward is that production will be curtailed. It is inconceivable, with $5 million less assistance being paid, that some mines will not find it necessary to close their doors.
The ministry may not see eye to eye with me on these figures, but the information I have is to the effect that in 1940 the number of mines in operation was 144, and that number had been reduced by 1954 to only 54 mines. I am speaking now of quartz mines; that figure does not include placer mines, as did the figure given by the minister. The . figure of 54 mines in 1954 may not be correct, but in any event the figure of 70 mines in 1954 which appears in the blue book does include placer mines, and, I believe, quite a number of them. It is clear that over the period there has been a substantial reduction in the number of quartz gold mines which have been in operation or which have been able to continue in operation, which would be a more accurate way of putting it.
I anticipate, and I think it is proper to anticipate, that this bill with its restrictive features will further curtail the number of mines in production, the amount of gold produced and the number of miners and

-a cut in gold assistance will doubtless reduce employment in the mines adversely affected, and also kill any urge there might previously have been to hunt for gold or to develop new gold mines. speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys

speechtext: May I ask the source of that quotation and the name of the person whose words are being quoted?

speechtext:
Yes. I am quoting a statement made by Mr. Bert W. Lang in a letter addressed to me. I believe he has written to all the members of the government and all the members of the house. He has made a careful analysis of the effect of the assistance on gold mining.
Although the minister hopes this measure will not close the high cost low grade mines which will still receive substantial assistance based on costs of $26.50, nevertheless the formula would substantially reduce the gold assistance in toto and also the gold assistance received by a number of lower cost high grade mines such as Kerr-Addison, McIntyre, Campbell Red Lake, New Dickenson, Leitch, Bonwhit, and others.
He continues:
I am certain that if this basis of gold assistance were adopted, that a mine like McIntyre, where gold assistance represents a large part of its yearly profit, would decide to curtail operations to a minimum to carry a small working force only, rather than continue to eat up their ore reserves with gold at the present price and thereby only recover a relatively small profit from such reserves. Such mines would much prefer to close down or reduce to a very small scale production in order to conserve ore reserves for the day which may not be too far ahead when the United States will be forced to increase the price of gold.
This assistance has been a very material consideration in the maintenance and operation of some of these mines. We have now dealt with the problem of the economics of ' mining, but there are some extremely cogent social reasons why this assistance has been a proper expedient during the past few years. One has only to think of the great gold mining communities so well represented by my hon. friend across the way, who will doubtless speak on this measure, to realize some of the implications of this bill. I am referring of course to the communities of Kirkland Lake, Porcupine and Timmins, which are purely gold camps. From such mines comes 88 per cent of the gold produced in Canada. The other 12 per cent comes 

from areas of mixed mining and presumably would not be affected by the removal of this subsidy.
The gold mining communities which produce 88 per cent of the gold in Canada depend now and have depended for some years upon this assistance.
The number of men directly employed is 18,800, according to figures released last November. The government in its speech from the throne indicated its desire to create more employment, and indicated that public works projects were to be undertaken for that purpose. We were led to believe projects would be undertaken to create work through the expenditure of public funds.
I think I have already mentioned this, but I ask again what more appropriate way there is of creating work through the use of public funds than by encouraging an industry which is non-competitive, in which overproduction is not possible and employment is substantial. The gold mining industry uses vast quantities of chemical and metal supplies of all kinds. Anyone who lived through the depressed period of the thirties realizes what a godsend the gold mining industry of Ontario was to that province, because it maintained itself and a great many subsidiary and collateral industries.
If this bill results in a reduction in the working force, which now totals 18,800 employed in the gold mining industry, certainly this will have to be offset if the government means what it says concerning the expenditure of funds for public works, not only to the extent of these subsidies but I think many times that amount to produce equivalent employment in other places. Not only would it be difficult to do that, but imagine the disruption of people who have their own homes, their own properties and are settled and rooted in those communities in the gold mining areas and have no desire to leave them.
I have mentioned the collateral benefits to agriculture and to industry-in fact to the whole economy-which supply communities of the size and importance of these gold mining areas.
I now come to the other and final reason for the importance of this subsidy. I hope I have not minimized or passed too quickly over the social and economic aspects of it, but I come now to the production of gold for its own sake. I should like to say something about that matter, because there are a great many people who seem to think gold has no "sake" any more. Actually I regard gold as the basic reserve of our money credit system.
The immediate result of this bill, or at least the immediate result of its predecessors,

has been to produce higher gold reserves in Canada. I have said that they have increased 73 per cent in seven years, and that is the amount of gold produced in that time. Our reserves are now over $1 billion in gold. Those are reserves that cannot be dug up and produced at will. At this time, if we allow some fruitless years to go by in gold mining we shall never make up the loss that will be incurred. The increase in reserves in the past four years in Canada-that is the total reserve of gold and United States dollars- has been only $200 million or 11 per cent, because gold has replaced United States dollars to some extent. At the same time the increase in capital investment in this country from abroad has been in the neighbourhood of $3 billion, or 35 per cent of our previous capital investment. It is therefore easy to see that our gold reserves or our gold and United States dollar reserves are not increasing in proportion to our outside investment.
Another practical way of looking at this production of gold, and one which will appeal to all who have any gambling instincts, is that although it is worth $35 today, by virtue of the United States maintaining that price, there is no saying that it will not be worth $70 two or three years hence. One can imagine what a tidy profit the treasury or the Minister of Finance would find in the gold reserve if the price were doubled overnight, as it might well be. I think that is something to be looked forward to not only with equanimity but with anticipation. If the odds on such an event are even-and I suggest they are better than that-the more gold we have in the till when that happens, the better off this country will be.

That is United States laws and regulations. -this country is on what may be termed an international gold bullion standard. We buy and sell gold freely with other countries through their central banks and treasuries at the price of $35 an ounce plus or minus a handling charge of one-fourth of 1 per cent.

The United States holds $22 billion of gold out of the world's monetary stock of gold of $36 billion. This huge stock of gold is a bulwark for confidence in the value of currency. In a world of great uncertainties it is one of the anchors of value on which business transactions depend.
He went on to refer to Fort Knox and what people think about it; then he said this:
In summary, this is our present gold policy: we are maintaining an assured ability to support a constant relationship between gold and the dollar- a relationship which is as important to foreign countries as it is to us.
He asked the question:
Can we safely now run the risk of letting both our own people and people elsewhere draw down this gold freely and perhaps dissipate it so that the strength of our monetary reserves is impaired?
Does that sound like the value depending on the unwilling purchase of gold by the United States?
It is the position of the treasury that it would not be wise to take the risk of a major step in relaxing restraints. We still live in a very uncertain world. A large part of the world's new gold production has been vanishing into gold hoards and becoming unavailable for monetary reserves.

That is the declared policy of United States treasury officials. The fact is that the United States over the past five years has sold and exported $3 billion of its gold reserves. Far from being the only purchaser, it has been a seller. The figures are given in the table which is attached to this document which I have just read, and they show a serious decline in the gold reserves held by the United States. As of 1939 the United States had $17,800 million of gold in reserve, of which $6 billion was the legal requirement as a backing for its currency. It held about $3 billion for foreign account. It therefore had a surplus over all requirements of about $8 billion.
Today that surplus has changed into a negative, for the simple reason that the $21 billion which the United States has in its gold reserve in Fort Knox is largely pledged for foreign account. As of November 30 last there was $12 billion, something over half, pledged to foreign account in the sense that it was security for short-term balances and was subject to withdrawal any time. So you can see that not only has there been a reduction in actual gold held from $24 billion to $21 billion in five years, that is a loss of $3 billion of the total holdings of gold in the United States, but there was as well an increase in the amount of these holdings of gold which were held for foreign accounts. Today the United States reserve of gold which it can really count on as a monetary reserve is down to something like $9 billion, not a very substantial amount.
On the contrary we find that European countries are building up their gold reserves again, and I should like to quote a dispatch from the Financial Times of a week ago under the name of Mr. DeSeau.
According to the organization for European economic co-operation, the western European trading nations, on December 31, 1954, held gold and dollar reserves of better than $13-5 billion.
As the position has been improving abroad we find a better international distribution of the gold reserves than existed immediately after the war, when there was such a concentration and unbalance in the United States.
Now, Mr. Speaker, that is by way of emphasis on the place of gold in our economy. I could spend some time referring to the international gold standard and discussing how it developed and what happened to it, but that is something we all know about. We know that in the 1930's it became politically impos-
[Mr. Michener.l

sible to maintain the discipline which was involved in the international gold standard, and so all countries departed from the practice of redeeming their paper money by gold and tried the much more pleasant and politically delightfully way of handling their obligations by so-called managed currency.
I should like to refer briefly to the disadvantages and political problems involved in the international gold standard. In that connection I quote the following from a paper on the monetary functions of gold:
During the 1930's especially it became politically impossible for any country to allow the fluctuations in income and employment which were essential to the gold standard. Commitment to a full employment policy and the implied rejection of international control over this "domestic" matter are incompatible with the functioning of an international gold standard. Governments can no longer afford politically to abide by the rules of the classical gold standard game.
Managed currency then was the vogue. It, of course, has its problems too, serious enough internally but far more complicated when one comes to an international financial system. One only has to look around a bit at the graveyard of managed currencies, which is full of rubles, marks and francs, to find that altogether it has not been quite as happy an episode in the financial history of modern times as its authors thought it would be. One can conceive of a managed currency in a stable world under one rule where one party had all the financial powers, but in a world which is at least in a cold war and under the possible threat of a third world war we have scarcely reached the conditions of unity and peace which lend themselves to managed international currency based on agreements and arrangements.
We know that even the international wheat agreement is difficult enough to negotiate and operate, and that the general agreement on tariffs and trade is also not easily retained even among the most civilized of people; and that is only part of the world. When it comes to a financial system to embrace the whole world it seems to me that one has to be a little more realistic than was Mr. Keynes in his doctrine which has been the inspiration of so much of this theorizing about monetary systems. I should like to quote the deputy minister of finance, and perhaps inquire whether the government's view of gold is his or his is the government's view. On May 11 last, In speaking to the Canadian political science association, he compared gold mining to coal mining. There is nothing wrong with that, and I am sure the hon.

member to my left will agree, but he regards them as not being dissimilar. He said:
It does not make sense to subsidize gold mining indefinitely.
I agree with that.
It does make sense as a transitional measure as long as there is some reasonable prospect of either the cost of mining going down or the price of gold going up. Unless there appears to be a fair chance of one or other of these things happening in the not too distant future, it would seem preferable to spend part of the present subsidy money on promoting an orderly and more rapid transfer of resources out of marginal gold mining and marginal gold mining communities.
Is that what the minister has in mind?
I suggest that the situation is nothing like as desperate as that, and I should like to offer as a counterblast the Wall Street Journal, which I am sure is subscribed to by most members of the house to my left to bring them back to sanity periodically.

This may seem like a dull and inconsequential piece of news. But it can prove one of the most significant economic things that has happened recently to Britain and the western trading world. And apart from its significance it is not without its drama. It marks a climax of what might be called the Keynes mutiny.
For a generation the economic thinking that has dominated the policies of our major governments has been that money can be successfully divorced from any tangible thing. It can be created by printing pieces of paper and these pieces of paper can be manipulated at will by the central authorities to make money do their bidding. This thinking was given impetus by the teachings of the late Lord Keynes, Britain's brilliant and articulate economic theorist, and his disciples.
In the thirties every major government abandoned the gold standard. The arguments were that a gold standard limited the quantity of money and therefore limited a government in doing all the nice things it ought to be doing for people. Money wasn't "flexible". By abandoning gold, government authorities would become the master instead of the slave of money.
The theorists also said that by arbitrarily fixing the price of one country's money relative to another, the planners could manage foreign trade to suit themselves. This was particularly appealing to Britain, whose economy depends so heavily on its position as a centre of world trade.
Well, it soon became apparent that gold did not die so easily. The governments had to prohibit anyone from exchanging money for gold, and vice versa, or else the open market would make a liar out of the governments.

I should like to urge the minister at this point to reconsider his formula. It seems to me that stability and reasonable permanence are needed if the gold mining industry is to go ahead with assurance, and if


there is to be the exploration and development that is necessary to keep it alive. I would like to deal briefly with a little of the history of gold mining in Canada. The contribution the industry has made to the national economy in earlier and more favourable circumstances, in creating new wealth, in affording steady employment, in stimulating other industries, and in opening up and developing northern Canada by establishing important towns and communities, is a well-known matter of record.
Since 1948 assistance to offset increasing costs has been paid to gold mines by the federal government under the authority of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. This assistance recognizes the fact that the abandonment of the gold standard, the fixing of the price of gold at $35 per ounce by the United States government, the period of managed currencies thereafter, and the unmanaged period of great inflation which has ensued-all, except the latter, done with a view to controlling the currency situation of the world in the absence of the gold standard-are, first of all temporary measures and, in the second place, have created immense burdens for the gold producers and gold producing countries, and the communities concerned.
As I say, I think these facts are generally known, but what is almost always forgotten is that the steps that were taken, that created a depressed industry out of the once great and flourishing gold mining industry, were in the national interest, and

Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act that a relatively small group of Canadians are bearing the entire load. There are all too many people who shrug and say, "Oh, well, why worry about gold? You can't eat it". They forget about the depression when we absorbed thousands of unemployed and created work in many factories throughout the whole of Canada by our purchase of supplies and materials. They forget that it was gold men and women, and gold money, that discovered and developed our great base metal mines and found our uranium mines.
There are also those who think that the importance of gold is a thing of the past; but as long as there is a ready market for every ounce that is produced; as long as the governments of the world feel that it is expedient for them to bolster their money with gold holdings, and as long as the general public cannot hold gold in a conveniently negotiable form, then I contend that gold must be as important, as a monetary metal, as it ever was.
Furthermore as an export product, nothing produced in Canada is more readily sold. Canada's entire output of gold could be sold to other countries to help balance our trade, and of course the present output could be multiplied with a more realistic price for gold-that is, provided we are not allowed to die. A gold mine is not like other business; if you close it down it simply becomes a hole in the ground, filled with water and in most cases too costly to open again, even with an increase in the price, except those mines with very high grade ores.
No manufacturer could stay in business if he had to sell his product at considerably less than he did 15 years ago, yet that is exactly the position the gold mines find themselves in today, without a subsidy. In 1940 they received $38.50 per ounce and on January 15 this year $33.79, or a drop of $4.71 per ounce. The recent changes in the exchange rate have made some slight improvement in this.
In this same period the costs of production have soared, as they have in every business. In fact from 1941 to 1952 the increase in cost was $7.78 per ounce. The drop in the price of gold during the same period was $4.23, making a total decrease in revenue per ounce of $12.01. During 1952 the average assistance paid under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was $3.14 per ounce. This represented about one-quarter of the actual loss per ounce to producers.
A large proportion of the increased cost was in increased wages to mine employees. A study of some 18 gold mines in Ontario

Another point that may be of interest is the fact that there are no lay-offs in this industry, seasonal or otherwise. The only time men are thrown out of employment is when the remaining ore cannot be mined at a profit under today's conditions. There is also very little turnover in labour. The Ontario mining association made a survey of 22 of the older gold mines in the province and found that of the 8,000-odd employees involved 37 [DOT] 9 per cent had service of over 10 years, 14 per cent from 10 to 15 years, 11-8 per cent from 15 to 20 years and 12 per cent over 20 years.
The gold mining industry currently affords steady employment to approximately 20,000 Canadians. Many of these are the heads of families and support a number of dependents. In addition it is estimated that for each man employed in a gold mine, four others are given employment in industries supplying the mines with goods and services. During 1952 the gold mines made major expenditures of more than $130 million. Any drastic curtailment in gold mining employment would have very serious effects on the general employment situation in Canada.


I had a survey made in my own camp in the Kirkland-Larder area. The mines purchased, in supplies, more than $5,500,000. These materials came from over 100 different towns, mostly in Ontario and Quebec but some from other provinces as well.
It will readily be seen that the effects, directly and indirectly, of any substantial reduction in gold mining employment are bound to have very serious repercussions on the national economy and would certainly require extensive and expensive measures of rehabilitation and relief. From British Columbia and the Northwest Territories, through Manitoba to northern Ontario and northwestern Quebec there is a chain of towns and communities which depend wholly or chiefly on gold mining activities. One of the principal purposes of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was to afford these communities the means of continued existence. It has been estimated that, exclusive of mining properties, the municipal valuation of these gold mining communities is of the order of $128 million.
It cannot be emphasized too strongly that the very existence of these communities and the welfare of their inhabitants depend' on gold mining activity. Any curtailment in this activity is immediately felt in terms of unemployment and depressed property values. Any measures which resulted in the closing of a substantial number of gold mines would be disastrous for these municipalities. The problems of rehabilitation and relief would be tremendous and very, very costly.
It should not be forgotten that these are the Canadians who opened up the great mineralized areas of Canada, this huge treasure house comprising almost two-thirds of the area of the whole country, with a future that makes Canada the envy of the whole world. It takes a special breed of man or woman to make a pioneer; it takes imagination, enthusiasm, vision and above all stamina. Everything most of us own is invested in these mining towns; in public utilities, schools, roads and in our homes. If it were not for the assistance as proposed in the amendment before us today many of the mines now operating would have no alternative but to close. I regret that the total assistance had to be reduced. The amount made available will, I hope, prevent any closures provided there is no drastic increase in the cost of operation.
The proposed assistance is being paid to prevent unemployment, and is based solely on the cost of producing an ounce of gold. All clauses that might stimulate production have been removed. I believe that the total amount available is to be distributed, under

the new formula, in the most equitable manner. I wish to congratulate the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys and his staff for their painstaking care in the drafting of the new formula.
Canada is not alone in providing assistance for the producers of gold during this trying period. The experience of other countries, faced in different degrees with the same dilemma, is instructive. Producers in South Africa and Australia gained relief and benefit not available to Canadian producers when their currencies were devalued in 1949; the effect at that time was to enable them to obtain a price for gold equivalent to $50 an ounce. The Australian government has instituted a subsidy plan for gold operators. A similar undertaking has been given to the gold producers of the Philippines. Before instituting assistance these countries came to Canada and studied our methods.
In conclusion I would like to read a telegram from the township of Teck, my own community:
On behalf of the citizens of this mining community, I respectfully request the favourable consideration by the government of the continuation of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. As you know, this community of 18,000 is dependent on the primary payroll of six producing gold mines within its municipal boundaries. Without the assistance provided by this act it is certain that the majority of these mines would close immediately and the subsequent operations of the others would be on a substantially reduced scale. Over 41 per cent of the total population of municipalities in the entire district of Timiskaming reside in Teck, which provides a ready market for much of the farm and dairy produce of the area. Should this community be permitted to die, due to the mines closing, the resulting economic and social disturbance in the whole district would create many problems for both federal and provincial governments. In addition to the immediate effect on this community and district, the further reduction in gold mining would seriously affect other industries supplying goods and services to the industry and community. The concern of the government for the welfare of this and other gold mining communities was clearly stated when the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was first considered in parliament and on the occasions when the measure was renewed in subsequent years. I wish to express the sincere appreciation of the community for this assistance and to request that the legislation be continued.
H. L. Cooper, Reeve, Township of Teck.
This telegram is typical of those I have received from all the municipalities concerned.
I am confident that this measure will receive the support of the hon. members of this house, as failure to provide at least the amount of assistance set out in the amendment would most certainly create unemployment, not only in gold mining communities but in other manufacturing centres as well.

In 1942 what was known as the reconstruction committee was set up in this house. I was a member of that committee. The job that was given to us was to plan post-war employment.
That committee dug very deeply into the realm of economics. Principal Cyril James of McGill University was an adviser to that committee. I remember the discussion on the subject of gold as a standard for our currency in the future. I remember Principal James' answer. He said that gold as the standard of currency was a thing of the past. He said it was his opinion that in the postwar years we would use gold to make wedding rings, to fill our teeth and so on. He said that our currency was measured by the productive capacity of the country, and unless we measured our currency in that way we would have inflation and deflation and burying gold in Fort Knox would not affect it very much.
However, he was not long on that committee. I do not know whether they removed him because of that statement, but he disappeared from the committee. I saw a lot of that man. I thought he was one of the most effective and impressive persons I had ever heard talking; and he knew his subject, any subject on which he wanted to talk. That was his opinion at that time, and it was worth something.
I heard the two hon. members speak, and I appreciate their plea for assistance to the industry. We are now dealing on second reading of the bill with the principle of subsidies, and with that principle I am not quarrelling. It is amazing to see how fast those who support exclusively the system of free enterprise shift their footwork and ask for measures to protect and assist an industry that gets into trouble.
In going to the extent they do with subsidies the government is not living up to some of the things it has said since 1945. For example, in the white paper tabled in the house
2188	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act by the Minister of Trade and Commerce at that time setting out policy, it was definitely stated that as far as the government was concerned free enterprise had a field that was free in which it could operate efficiently and effectively; but that in any sector of our society where free enterprise did not measure up and do the job it should do, the government would step in and take over.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Does he consider free enterprise one that has a controlled price in the national interest?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: No, certainly I do not. That is not free enterprise. That is exactly my argument. Those who stick so vehemently to the theory of free enterprise are so willing to adopt socialist measures in order to help it out as long as the profits go to the people they support. That is the thing which amazes me, because if I were a Conservative and I stood for the policies-

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: You should be.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: -of the Conservative party I would oppose subsidization as a socialist measure, but they are advocating it. The hon. member for St. Paul's has done an excellent job tonight. If I did not know where he sat in this house and closed my eyes I would say to myself, "This fellow is on the road to socialism."

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: I agree it does not make sense.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext:
So far as I am concerned I approve of the measure because of the value it is to the mining community, the number of people for whom it provides a livelihood, the support it gives the community. Based on the principle of subsidy to an industry in that kind of trouble under the present scheme of things, the government is doing exactly what it should do; it is considering the community and the people who live in it.
The -subsidy is not the only assistance the gold industry receives. The two hon. members who have just spoken would lead you to believe that the $65,441,904.84 received from 1948 to 1953 and the 1954-55 estimate of nearly $16 million was the sum total of the assistance. That is not correct. New mines are given an exemption period of three years during which they do not have to pay corporate income tax. That is assistance. A mining company is granted depletion allowances, which means that 40 per cent of the net profit is exempt from tax. That is assistance. Mining companies, like oil companies, may


now charge capital exploration charges directly to the profit and loss account. Ordinarily the only charges allowed against income are those which have been incurred directly in the earning of that income. That is not so in the case of the mining companies.
The federal government assists these industrial dependents in other ways, such as special freight rates and the provision of services rendered by the department of mines, such as geological surveys, the development of milling processes, etc. That is all assistance. Provincial governments assist them by offering preferred hydroelectric rates and by providing provincial grants to the municipalities in lieu of taxes which the mining companies are not required to pay. That is all assistance.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit me a question?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Surely.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member is suggesting that this assistance is given only to gold mines. Similar assistance is given to agriculture and other industries. This assistance is shared in, not something special.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: I do not know who else gets it. The oil companies receive a lot.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit another question? In what province do the gold mines receive a preferred hydro rate?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: In the province of Ontario.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: I beg your pardon, sir; they do not.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Well, I have a brief here which supports my statement. You do know that the Ontario legislature appointed a special commission in November, 1954, to inquire into the gold mining industry? You know that?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Indeed.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: You know that the steel workers' union did extensive research and made a presentation to the commission, which consisted of three professors? I went through that brief presented by the steel workers' union. Their evidence was accepted by the commission. It is from their evidence given to the commission in November, 1954, that I have taken the details of the assistance which I am pointing out now, and I am reasonably sure that the brief was factual.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: And I am reasonably sure it is not.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: You argue that point with Charlie Millard the first time you meet him.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: That would be a pleasure.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext:
Now to continue with the subsidy business, many companies escape a major share of the municipal taxation which every other industry must bear. Municipalities, in Ontario at least, are permitted by provincial statute to assess only the value of the surface property of the mine. The province reimburses the municipalities in part for the loss of these revenues. Even with these grants mining municipalities receive much less than a fair and just revenue from their chief industry. It is generally conceded in Ontario urban municipalities that industry should bear about 40 per cent of municipal taxes. In 1954 the revenue from all industry, including the provincial mines grant, was only 13-7 per cent of the total revenue of the town of Timmins. In other words not only is the federal government subsidizing the gold mining industry, but provincial and municipal governments are also subsidizing it.
Nor is this all; the miners themselves are contributing a substantial subsidy every year to the gold mining industry. The miners' subsidy is paid in the form of lower wages, longer hours, greater occupational risks, fewer holidays with pay and less fringe benefits than workers in any other comparable industry. To find the extent to which employees are subsidizing the gold mining industry we have only to compare wages, hours, and working conditions of gold mines with those of metal mining other than gold.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: What about coal?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext:
Coal is worse. That is my battle all the time, and it will be for some time to come. In 1946 wages, hours and conditions in gold mining were approximately equal to those in other metal mining. Since then the conditions of the gold miners have continuously deteriorated. In 1946 wages in gold and other metal mining were about equal. By 1949 wages in metal mining industries were on the average 128 per cent of the average hourly wages in gold mining. By 1953 average hourly wages in other metal mining had increased to 156 per cent of the average hourly wage in gold mining. Between 1949 and 1953 hourly wages in gold mines increased by 20-6 per cent. Hourly wages in other metal mining increased during the same period by 46-2 per cent. Gold miners still work 48 hours or more per week, while 87 per cent of other metal miners have a 40-hour week.
No gold mines allow more than five statutory holidays in a year. Some 77-6 per cent of employees in Canadian manufacturing industries are paid for six or more, while 50 [DOT] 5 per cent are paid for eight or more. In
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act vacation plans gold mining is far behind other metal mining. In the gold mining industry only 3 [DOT] 1 per cent of employees get two weeks' vacation with pay after three years' service or less. In other metal mining 92 * 9 per cent receive two weeks' vacation with pay after three years' service. In other metal mining 86-9 per cent receive three weeks with pay after 20 years' employment. No gold miner is ever granted three weeks' vacation with pay, no matter how long he works.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Several of those statements are absolutely inaccurate. What is the source of your information?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: You get in touch with that commission before it makes its report.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: I have read all of them.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext:
This is the evidence they have. As to pension plans, 26-6 per cent of gold mine employees enjoy the benefit of pension plans but 86-9 per cent of employees in other metal mining enjoy such plans. Mr. Justice W. D. Roach of the supreme court of Ontario, in a conciliation board report dated August 18, 1953, in a dispute between the International Nickel Company and the mine, mill and smelter workers' union, stated that the wages paid by the company were adequate merely to support a family of two. The gold mines are paying 30 per cent less on an average than the International Nickel Company was then paying.
The demands of the mining industry upon the federal treasury warrant the setting up of a royal commission to investigate the entire gold mining industry. I think such an investigation would be good for everybody.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Surely.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Like my friend the hon. member for Timiskaming I should like to disagree with some of the figures but I do not want to do so now, because I do not want to interrupt. However, I should like to ask this question. Does the hon. member appreciate the fact that the amount of the reduction in subsidy provided for in this bill, namely $5 million, if interpreted in terms of wages would be about $260 per man per year in the gold mining industry, if the government goes ahead with the reduction? I do not say that it will mean a reduction in wages but that, if interpreted in wages, that is what it amounts to.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext:
I am not arguing that point at all. I do not think you can build up wage rates with subsidies. But if it takes an increase in subsidy in order to give the
2190	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act people who dig that ore out of the ground a decent standard of living, then I am in favour of increasing that subsidy. As long as that industry is considered to be necessary to the economy of Canada, I believe in holding it up. If it requires more money in order to put the gold miners on the same footing as people who do equal work-for example, the people in Sudbury who dig nickel out of the ground-then I think it should be provided. I think those employed in gold mining should be on a par with them because the work is equal.
I am not quarrelling with the subsidy at all. As long as we admit that it is necessary to use public funds in order to maintain that industry in the interests of the community and the people in it, I am not quarrelling about the amount of the subsidy. What I am saying, however, is this. Paying that subsidy to the industry alone, just to be used for their own purposes, and ignoring the conditions and circumstances under which the people live who dig that gold is not the proper thing to do. I think a share of the money that is paid by way of subsidy definitely should be earmarked in order to give those who dig the ore a decent standard of living. That is my argument.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? I just showed that more than the subsidy has been paid out in increased wages. How can the hon. member imply that the subsidy is used for the benefit of the operators?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: May I say to the hon. member that I do not know how she could verify the figures she put on the record.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: I can submit annual statements and audited accounts.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: I should like to tell the hon. member that my experience has been this. For a good many years before I came into the house it was my unfortunate duty to be obliged to go in and argue wage rates across the table with a bigger company than any of those in the gold mining industry, but one that was much of the same type. From their balance sheets and from their public statements nobody could get any figures that would give any kind of a picture of what that company was doing.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Oh, nonsense.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext:
Just a minute. We have had the experience of signing a contract that had a profit-sharing clause in it. We were


going to share the profits with a big organization. After two years of working under that profit-sharing plan we brought in an auditor. We brought him from Mexico so he would be free and independent. He was internationally known. He was one of the best in the country. He worked on their books for six months. He then came back and reported that no auditor or no one in the world could get any kind of statement as to profit or loss, wages or what the charges were from the books kept by the company. They kept two sets of books, one for their own private information and one for public consumption. He could not do anything with them. He threw up his hands and left. The hon. member may think the balance sheets and statements issued by these people can be accepted at face value, but I know they cannot be so accepted.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Would the hon. member believe our treasury department? They audit all the accounts.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: They see the accounts that are given them, but they do not know whether they have half of them or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Oh, yes, they do.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext:
Oh, no. Ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) who had to handle the subsidies to these big organizations during the war. Sit down and have a private talk with him some day and see what his experience was.
Let us get back, Mr. Speaker, to the subject matter under discussion. In the interests of the people who dig the gold there are certain things that should be done. Two good arguments have been made for the operators, and I am just trying to balance and round the thing out.
I believe this subsidy should be granted on the following conditions. First, I think the difference between wages and working conditions in the gold mines and those in other metal mines should be eliminated. In the second place, since labour conditions and collective bargaining procedures are matters of provincial jurisdiction, this government should seek an agreement with the provincial governments whereby necessary and effective provincial legislation may be secured regarding both minimum wages and collective bargaining procedures.
A welfare fund for miners should be established, financed by the employers and administered by a tripartite board of trustees representing employer, union and government, in order to provide a form of severance

compensation to workers who must retire from mine employment because of old age, exhaustion of the ore bodies or ill health.
I might say that in the coal mines we have had that type of thing for many years and it works well.
Adequate and effective action must be taken by the mine employers and by the responsible agencies of government in order to improve the living and working conditions of miners and to eliminate the hazards of sickness and accident.
A joint federal-provincial training and educational program should be expedited in the gold mining regions in order to help the unemployed workers develop the skills which are required for expanding industries, especially for those new industries which are to be established in the region. I might say that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) has that type of organization in his own riding today, for retraining the textile workers who were laid off en masse there. I think a similar type of organization should be established not only in the gold mining industry but also in the coal mining industry. I know the minister's department is working on a general scheme of that kind. I hope the gold mining regions will not be forgotten if and when it becomes national policy.
Special attention must be given by the provincial and federal governments to the location and development of more diversified industries in the regions now heavily dependent upon gold mining, particularly the Porcupine and Kirkland Lake districts. I think the hon. member will agree with me that both gold mining and coal mining reach a peak; they peter out, and the communities wind up as ghost towns. Before that situation comes about, steps should be taken to establish some type of industry that is suitable to that locality, and to retrain men who may be weeded out of industry for the reasons that I have mentioned.
That is something that should be done so these communities may not go down. When the gold mines run out, as the coal mines have done and will continue to do, we should have some type of diversified industries based on what that particular part of the country is able to support, so that the churches and schools and homes may not be lost and these towns may not become ghost towns. I think it is well to look ahead to that sort of thing.
I think improved and more effective techniques must be developed and applied by the
18, 1955	2191
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act national employment service in order to facilitate the placement of unemployed and underemployed workers in expanding industries. Financial aid supplementary to and different in purpose from unemployment insurance compensation would help to mitigate, to some extent, the hardships and difficulties of adaptation to industrial and occupational changes in employment.
Geographical labour force transfers present human, social and financial problems and therefore should be avoided where more attractive alternatives can be made available. However, those workers who want to move to industrial areas where employment opportunities are more attractive and more abundant should be given greater financial help. The need for such help is much greater in the northern regions where the costs, risks and uncertainties of moving and re-establishing a family and household are greater. This is so because of the dependence upon a few concentrated employment centres sparsely scattered over very wide distances, and because of the dependence upon a very limited number of resource-exhausting staple industries.
In the few minutes left I should like to say that one of the greatest problems in the north country is that of the worker 40 years of age and over. I may tell the hon. member for Timiskaming that I have spent some time in that territory, and I know what the people are up against. They have always had my sympathy and help in any way I could help them. One of the greatest problems I saw there was that of workers 40 years of age and over. There were so many of them who became unemployed and, because the work was heavy and hazardous, employers were reluctant to take them back. The same is true of the coal mine operators and the nickel people. The country seemed to be full of these men, and they are pathetic figures.
The second point I think should be taken under consideration is the incidence of silicosis. You do not get silicosis in the coal mines; you get anthracosis, which is a different thing and not as bad. But in the metal mines the miners breathe the rock dust which is full of silica, and the disease comes on them insidiously. They begin to feel lazy and drowsy, and realize there is something the matter. They go to the hospital and are X-rayed, but the disease is pretty hard to detect because there are so many different types of chest conditions. But when the disease gets a good solid hold on them
2192	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act they see a doctor and he suspects that they may have it. Of course if it is diagnosed as silicosis it is compensable and the men receive compensation.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: It is pretty well under control now.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: No.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Oh, yes, it is.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Oh, no, it is not. The difficulty I found in the north country, and we run into it in our own part of the country, is that a diagnosis is not made. The doctors will quibble about it, and then the second stage is tuberculosis.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Stage?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Exactly. If you let silicosis go on long enough, if it is not detected soon enough, it will turn to tuberculosis and then it is not compensable.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: Is the hon. member not aware that silicosis is a disease that is only developed through breathing silica, and that tuberculosis cannot be developed unless you come in contact with the germ? Furthermore, is the hon. member not aware that at least in the province of Ontario if a miner who has silicosis should subsequently contact and develop tuberculosis that is also compensable?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: That last statement is news to me. I want to inform the hon. member that I went through that part of her province.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: A long time ago.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext:
I was in Kirkland Lake in 1941, and I met a man there who had had silicosis for a considerable time. The doctors finally diagnosed his condition as tuberculosis. The man was dying, and in order to protect his family so far as compensation was concerned we advised the man to will his body to his friend, who would see that the body was dissected after the man died in order to prove that he had died from silicosis so his family might receive the compensation pension that he should have been receiving during the years he was struggling along, going from silicosis to tuberculosis.
I have had a lot of experience with this business, both in the coal mines and in the metal mines. I am not so sure but what I have it myself. I want to tell you that after we had that man's body dissected and got the autopsy report we found it stated definitely that while the man had died finally from tuberculosis, he had suffered for some


years from silicosis. As a result the widow and children received the compensation pension.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: That was under a Liberal government in Ontario.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext:
That was in 1941. Of course there have been legislative changes in the years since. It was not even in the compensation act then as a compensable disease, but it is today. It has been said that miners do not get silicosis in coal mines. There is a lot of rock blasting and drilling in coal mines also, and some people do pick up the disease. It is one of the most difficult things to detect, because it is well advanced before there is an opportunity to discover what it is.
I have checked with a good many doctors. In fact we convened dozens of them and got their opinion en bloc on the question. I want to say now that the methods used in the province of Ontario, in my own province and in British Columbia so far as the diagnosis of silicosis is concerned are almost as inadequate today as they were in 1941. I can take you to my province. I have not been up your way since 19-

speechtext: -48. I can take you to my province and show you many men who in my judgment and in the judgment of the local doctor have silicosis. They have been idle for three years, and they are still fighting to prove they have the disability. The compensation doctor says they have not got it. The papers are sent to Dr. Riddell in Toronto, who is looked upon as the final authority. X-rays and reports are sent to him. The local doctor will say the man has the disease, the compensation doctor will say he has not, and in most cases I have seen Dr. Riddell will agree with the compensation doctor in the province of Nova Scotia. When the minister is concluding the subsidy arrangements I hope he will also take a look at the men who dig the gold, and see if something cannot be done for them.

In the present circumstances of the industry I have no objection to helping it by way of subsidy, but I do insist that the man who goes underground, breathes silica dust and takes the risk is also entitled to compensation. I hope the day will come in this and every other country when every last man can be taken from underground and the shafts can be sealed. It is no place to earn a living. I hope these men can some day be placed in factories and plants where they can enjoy the sunshine and fresh air, and work at production that is useful to mankind.
